zettels.title: My writing influences
zettels.mainIdea: My work is influenced by character-centered and philosophical speculative fiction in the tradition of Gene Roddenberry, H. G. Wells, Isaac Asimov, Orson Scott Card, Kurt Vonnegut Jr., Stephen King, and T. C. Southwell, blending present-day realism with alien contact, apocalyptic survival, moral consequence, and psychological transformation.
zettels.body:
My writing draws from the character-centered and philosophical speculative-fiction traditions associated with Gene Roddenberry, H. G. Wells, Isaac Asimov, Orson Scott Card, Kurt Vonnegut Jr., Stephen King, and T. C. Southwell.

These influences shape how I blend realistic present-day settings with speculative elements such as alien contact, apocalyptic survival, moral consequence, and psychological transformation.

zettels.title: Culinary influences
zettels.mainIdea: My culinary perspective develops through the chefs, writers, cultures, traditions, experiences, and ideas that shape how I understand food and cooking.
zettels.body:
Culinary influences are not limited to copying another chef’s recipes, techniques, or style. They include the people, cultures, ingredients, traditions, experiences, and systems of thought that affect how I approach food.

An influence may shape how I build flavor, choose ingredients, understand technique, develop recipes, construct menus, present food, or communicate culinary ideas. These influences become part of my perspective, but they are interpreted through my own experiences, cultural background, judgment, and creative process.

Samin Nosrat is one of these influences because her teaching emphasizes understanding the foundational elements of cooking rather than relying only on recipes.
futureUse: culinary philosophy, essays, recipe development, menu development, teaching, Fresh Roots Flavor Kitchen
questions: How has each culinary influence changed my understanding of food?
Which influences support my existing culinary philosophy?
How do I acknowledge influence without imitating another person’s work?

zettels.title: Flavor development
zettels.mainIdea: Flavor development is the deliberate process of building, balancing, concentrating, layering, and connecting flavors throughout preparation and cooking.
zettels.body:
Flavor development does not happen only when seasoning is added at the end of cooking. It begins with ingredient selection and continues through preparation, seasoning, cooking technique, temperature, timing, texture, and finishing.

Each stage can alter how an ingredient tastes. Browning can create depth, reduction can concentrate flavor, acid can add brightness, salt can improve clarity, fat can carry flavor, and heat can transform aroma, texture, and intensity.

Developing flavor requires understanding how individual elements interact rather than treating seasoning as a single final adjustment. The goal is not always to make flavor stronger. The goal may be balance, contrast, clarity, depth, restraint, or harmony.
futureUse: recipe development, menu development, culinary essays, cooking methods, flavor analysis, teaching
questions: At what stages is flavor being developed?
Does the dish need depth, contrast, brightness, concentration, or restraint?
How do technique and timing change the final flavor?

zettels.title: Intuitive Cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Intuitive cooking is the ability to make informed culinary decisions by observing ingredients, understanding principles, tasting, and responding to what is happening during the cooking process.
zettels.body:
Intuitive cooking is not cooking without knowledge or preparation. It develops through experience, observation, repetition, tasting, and an understanding of how ingredients and techniques behave.

A recipe may provide structure, but the cook must still respond to differences in ingredients, equipment, temperature, timing, moisture, seasoning, and personal intention. The same written instruction may produce different results under different conditions.

Cooking intuitively means recognizing these changes and adjusting with purpose. It involves knowing when food needs more salt, acid, fat, heat, moisture, time, texture, or restraint.

Samin Nosrat’s approach supports this way of thinking by teaching foundational elements that can be applied beyond a single recipe.
futureUse: recipe development, culinary teaching, personal cooking philosophy, essays, kitchen training
questions: What observations should guide an adjustment?
When should a recipe be followed exactly, and when should it be adapted?
How can intuitive decisions be explained clearly to another cook?

zettels.title: Salt as a foundational element of cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Salt develops and clarifies flavor when its type, quantity, timing, distribution, and relationship to the other elements of a dish are understood.
zettels.body:
Salt does more than make food taste salty. It can reveal existing flavors, reduce the perception of bitterness, influence moisture, affect texture, and help separate indistinct flavors.

The result depends on when salt is introduced, how evenly it is distributed, what kind of salt is used, and how it interacts with the ingredients. Seasoning during different stages can produce a more integrated result than relying only on final seasoning.

Salt must be evaluated within the entire dish. Ingredients such as cured meats, cheeses, sauces, stocks, and condiments may already contribute salt. Proper seasoning therefore requires tasting and considering every component together.
questions: When should the ingredient or dish be salted?
Which components already contribute salt?
Is the salt revealing flavor or overwhelming it?
How does the type of salt affect measurement and distribution?

zettels.title: Fat as a foundational element of cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Fat carries flavor, creates texture, transfers heat, adds richness, and shapes how a dish feels and tastes.
zettels.body:
Fat performs several culinary functions. It can carry aromatic compounds, provide richness, affect tenderness, create crispness, produce emulsions, and transfer heat during cooking.

Different fats contribute different flavors and behave differently under heat. Butter, olive oil, coconut milk, animal fats, seed oils, dairy, nuts, and other fat sources cannot always be treated as interchangeable.

The amount and type of fat should support the purpose of the dish. Too little may leave a dish dry, thin, or incomplete. Too much may suppress clarity or make the dish feel heavy. Acid, salt, heat, texture, and moisture can affect how richness is perceived.
questions: What function is the fat performing?
What flavor does the selected fat contribute?
Does the dish need richness, tenderness, crispness, or emulsification?
What balances the richness of the fat?

zettels.title: Acid as a foundational element of cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Acid creates brightness, contrast, structure, and balance while changing how salt, sweetness, bitterness, richness, and other flavors are perceived.
zettels.body:
Acid can brighten a dish, balance richness, sharpen indistinct flavors, and create contrast. It may come from citrus, vinegar, fermented ingredients, cultured dairy, fruit, wine, tomatoes, or other acidic foods.

Different acids have distinct flavors and intensities. They should therefore be selected according to the ingredients, cooking method, and intended character of the dish.

Acid can be introduced during cooking or used as a finishing element. Its timing affects whether it becomes integrated, softened, concentrated, or clearly noticeable. The purpose is not simply to make food sour, but to create balance and definition.
questions: What kind of acid belongs with these ingredients?
Should the acid be cooked or added at the end?
Is the dish lacking brightness, contrast, or balance?
How does the acid interact with sweetness, salt, bitterness, and fat?

zettels.title: Heat as a foundational element of cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Heat transforms ingredients, and controlling its source, intensity, duration, and distribution determines flavor, texture, moisture, and structure.
zettels.body:
Heat is not only a temperature setting. It includes how energy reaches food, how intensely it is applied, how evenly it is distributed, and how long the ingredient is exposed to it.

Different methods—such as roasting, frying, steaming, simmering, grilling, baking, and braising—produce different transformations. Heat can brown surfaces, soften fibers, evaporate moisture, render fat, set proteins, create crusts, or slowly develop tenderness.

Successful heat control requires attention to the ingredient, desired result, equipment, size, moisture level, and cooking stage. Higher heat is not always faster in a useful way, and lower heat is not always gentler. The correct heat is the heat that produces the intended transformation.
questions: What transformation should the heat produce?
How should heat reach the ingredient?
Does the ingredient require intensity, control, time, or a combination of them?
How are moisture and texture changing during cooking?

zettels.title: Flavor pairing
zettels.mainIdea: Flavor pairing is the deliberate combination of ingredients whose tastes, aromas, textures, and culinary functions support, contrast with, or transform one another.
zettels.body:
Flavor pairing involves more than identifying ingredients that taste good together. A pairing may work because ingredients share aromatic characteristics, create contrast, balance one another, or perform complementary roles within a dish.

Some pairings reinforce similar flavors, while others create interest through differences such as sweet and bitter, rich and acidic, soft and crisp, or earthy and bright. Cultural traditions, ingredient seasonality, cooking techniques, and personal experience also influence whether a combination feels coherent.

Flavor-pairing references can provide useful starting points, but they do not replace tasting or culinary judgment. A pairing must still be evaluated within the complete dish, including proportion, preparation, texture, temperature, seasoning, and intended experience.
questions: What makes these ingredients compatible?
Does the pairing rely on similarity, contrast, balance, or transformation?
How do proportion and preparation affect the pairing?
Does the combination support the intention of the dish?

zettels.title: Aromatic compounds in cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Aromatic compounds contribute to how ingredients smell and taste, and understanding their relationships can support ingredient pairing and flavor development.
zettels.body:
Aroma forms a major part of flavor perception. Ingredients contain volatile aromatic compounds that are released, altered, concentrated, or lost through cutting, crushing, heating, fermenting, drying, and other culinary processes.

Ingredients that share certain aromatic compounds may form useful pairings, but shared compounds do not guarantee that a combination will work. Taste, texture, intensity, preparation, cultural context, and the overall structure of the dish remain important.

Aromatic-compound information can be used as a tool for exploration. It may suggest unexpected ingredient relationships or help explain familiar combinations, but the final decision must still be tested through cooking and tasting.
questions: Which aromatic qualities are shared by these ingredients?
How does cooking alter their aromas?
Are the shared compounds noticeable in the finished dish?
What other factors determine whether the pairing works?

zettels.title: Ingredient Affinities
zettels.mainIdea: Ingredient affinities are recurring relationships between foods, seasonings, techniques, and flavor elements that work together within a culinary context.
zettels.body:
An ingredient affinity describes a meaningful culinary relationship between ingredients. These relationships may be based on shared aromas, complementary tastes, traditional use, seasonal availability, regional cuisine, texture, cooking technique, or repeated practical success.

Affinities can help identify ingredients that may support a central component of a dish. They can also reveal contrasting elements that provide balance, such as acid with richness or bitterness with sweetness.

An affinity should not be treated as a mandatory combination. It is a guide for exploration. The cook must still decide how much of each ingredient to use, how each component should be prepared, and whether the relationship supports the intended dish.
questions: What ingredients have an affinity with the central ingredient?
Why does the relationship work?
Is the affinity traditional, scientific, sensory, or contextual?
How can the combination be expressed without becoming predictable?

zettels.title: Food science in cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Food science helps explain how ingredients change during preparation and cooking, allowing culinary decisions to be made with greater understanding and control.
zettels.body:
Food science examines the physical and chemical changes that occur in ingredients. These changes include browning, protein coagulation, starch gelatinization, emulsification, fermentation, moisture movement, fat crystallization, and the release or loss of aromatic compounds.

Understanding these processes can help explain why a technique succeeds or fails. It can support decisions about temperature, timing, ingredient ratios, equipment, texture, and preservation.

Scientific knowledge should support culinary judgment rather than replace it. A technically correct process must still produce food that tastes good, has the intended texture, reflects its cultural context, and serves the purpose of the dish.
questions: What physical or chemical change is occurring?
How do temperature and time affect the result?
Which variables can be controlled?
How does scientific understanding improve the dish without limiting creativity?

zettels.title: Culinary Experimentation
zettels.mainIdea: Culinary experimentation is a structured process of testing ingredients, techniques, proportions, and ideas to discover how they affect a dish.
zettels.body:
Culinary experimentation allows ideas to be tested rather than accepted only in theory. An experiment may examine an ingredient pairing, cooking method, seasoning level, texture, temperature, substitution, or presentation.

Useful experimentation requires a clear purpose. Changing too many variables at once can make it difficult to understand what caused the result. Testing one major change at a time can produce more useful observations.

The outcome does not need to be successful to have value. An unsuccessful test can reveal problems with proportion, technique, timing, balance, or the original assumption. Recording observations makes the experiment useful for future recipe development and prevents the same test from being repeated without learning.
questions: What idea or assumption is being tested?
Which variable should change?
What result would support or challenge the idea?
What should be recorded after the test?

zettels.title: Recipe Development
zettels.mainIdea: Recipe development transforms a culinary idea into a repeatable preparation through research, testing, observation, adjustment, and clear documentation.
zettels.body:
Recipe development begins with an intention. The purpose may be to express an ingredient, reproduce a specific result, solve a culinary problem, explore a cultural connection, or create a new dish.

The process includes selecting ingredients, establishing proportions, choosing techniques, testing preparation steps, evaluating flavor and texture, and revising the recipe. Each change should be recorded so that the effect can be understood.

A developed recipe must communicate more than a list of ingredients. It should provide enough information for the intended cook to reproduce the result while still accounting for natural variation in ingredients, equipment, and environment.

A recipe may continue to evolve after it becomes usable. Development is complete when the recipe consistently produces the intended result, not merely when it works once.
questions: What is the intended result of the recipe?
Which variables require testing?
Can the result be reproduced consistently?
Are the instructions clear for the intended cook?
What remains unresolved after testing?

zettels.title: Taste and Aroma
zettels.mainIdea: Flavor emerges through the combined perception of taste and aroma, shaped further by texture, temperature, sound, memory, and expectation.
zettels.body:
Taste and aroma are connected but distinct parts of flavor perception. Taste identifies fundamental sensations such as sweetness, sourness, saltiness, bitterness, and umami. Aroma contributes the wider range of recognizable characteristics associated with ingredients, spices, herbs, roasting, fermentation, smoke, fruit, and other foods.

Aroma reaches perception through the nose before food enters the mouth and also while food is being chewed. Temperature, fat, moisture, cooking method, and ingredient structure influence how aromatic compounds are released.

Flavor cannot always be understood by examining taste alone. A dish may have appropriate salt, acid, sweetness, or bitterness but still seem incomplete if its aroma lacks clarity or depth. Likewise, strong aroma cannot correct poor balance or unpleasant texture.
questions: Which sensations come from taste and which come from aroma?
How does temperature affect aroma release?
What aromas define the central ingredients?
Does the aroma support the intended flavor experience?
How do memory and expectation influence perception?

zettels.title: Molecular Gastronomy
zettels.mainIdea: Molecular gastronomy studies the physical and chemical changes that occur during cooking and uses that knowledge to understand, test, and control culinary processes.
zettels.body:
Molecular gastronomy examines what happens to ingredients during preparation, cooking, cooling, storage, and consumption. It focuses on processes such as protein denaturation, emulsification, gelation, crystallization, fermentation, evaporation, pressure, temperature change, and the movement of moisture.

It is not limited to unusual presentations or modern restaurant techniques. Its broader purpose is to understand why culinary transformations occur and how variables such as temperature, time, ingredient ratios, acidity, pressure, and mechanical action affect the result.

Techniques commonly associated with molecular gastronomy include spherification, foams, gels, fluid gels, emulsions, sous vide cooking, rapid freezing, dehydration, and the use of hydrocolloids. These techniques are applications of scientific principles, but molecular gastronomy itself is the study of the processes behind cooking.

Scientific knowledge can help explain failures, improve consistency, create new textures, and support culinary experimentation. It should remain connected to taste, cultural context, ingredient purpose, and the intended dining experience rather than being used only for novelty.
questions: What physical or chemical process is occurring?
Which variables control the result?
How can the process improve consistency or understanding?
Does the technique improve the dish or only add novelty?
How does the process affect flavor, texture, aroma, and appearance?

zettels.title: Culinary Ratios
zettels.mainIdea: Culinary ratios express the proportional relationships between ingredients that create the underlying structure of a preparation.
zettels.body:
A culinary ratio identifies how ingredient quantities relate to one another rather than treating each quantity as an isolated measurement. Ratios can reveal the structure shared by preparations such as doughs, batters, custards, stocks, sauces, brines, and emulsions.

Understanding a ratio allows a cook to increase or decrease a preparation while preserving the intended relationship between ingredients. It can also make it easier to compare recipes, identify variations, and understand how changing one component affects the final result.

A ratio is a structural guide rather than a guarantee. Ingredient properties, technique, temperature, equipment, humidity, and the intended result may still require adjustment.
questions: Which ingredients define the core ratio?
Is the ratio based on weight, volume, or count?
Which ingredients can change without altering the structure?
What variables require adjustment beyond the ratio?

zettels.title: Recipe Scaling
zettels.mainIdea: Recipe scaling changes the yield of a preparation while preserving the necessary relationships between ingredients, technique, equipment, and cooking conditions.
zettels.body:
Recipe scaling involves more than multiplying or dividing every ingredient by the same number. Proportional calculation is the starting point, but the final result may also be affected by equipment size, surface area, cooking time, heat transfer, evaporation, mixing capacity, and ingredient behavior.

Some ingredients scale directly, while others may require judgment. Seasonings, leavening agents, thickeners, stabilizers, and highly concentrated ingredients may need to be evaluated rather than adjusted mechanically.

A properly scaled recipe should preserve the intended flavor, texture, structure, and yield. The revised version should be tested and documented rather than assumed to perform exactly like the original batch.
questions: What is the original yield?
What yield is required?
Which ingredients scale directly?
Will the equipment support the new batch size?
How might cooking time or heat transfer change?

zettels.title: Formula-Based Cooking
zettels.mainIdea: Formula-based cooking uses proportional structures and functional relationships to build preparations without depending entirely on one fixed recipe.
zettels.body:
Formula-based cooking begins with an understanding of the roles ingredients perform within a preparation. A formula may define the proportion of flour to liquid, fat to flour, salt to water, or another relationship that gives the preparation its basic structure.

Once the structure is understood, ingredients may be adapted according to flavor, purpose, availability, dietary needs, or desired texture. This supports creativity while preserving the relationships necessary for the preparation to function.

A formula is not the same as an unrestricted substitution system. Changes in ingredient composition can affect moisture, protein, starch, fat, sweetness, acidity, and cooking behavior. Variations must therefore be evaluated through testing
questions: What is the foundational formula?
What function does each ingredient perform?
Which components can be varied safely?
How does a substitution affect the structure?
What testing is needed before the formula is reliable?

zettels.title: Ingredient Proportions
zettels.mainIdea: Ingredient proportions determine how the components of a preparation interact and influence its flavor, texture, structure, moisture, and stability.
zettels.body:
Ingredient proportions describe the quantitative relationship between the parts of a preparation. These relationships can determine whether a mixture is firm or soft, rich or lean, thick or thin, stable or separated, balanced or overpowering.

Changing one ingredient may affect the functions of several others. Increasing liquid may require additional structure. Increasing fat may change tenderness or emulsification. Increasing sugar may affect sweetness, moisture, browning, and texture.

Proportions should therefore be considered according to both quantity and function. A successful preparation depends not only on how much of each ingredient is present but also on how those ingredients behave together.
questions: What function does each ingredient perform?
Which proportion controls the structure?
What happens when one component increases or decreases?
Are the proportions measured consistently?
Which relationships must remain stable?

zettels.title: Understanding Recipes Through Structure
zettels.mainIdea: A recipe can be understood as a structured system of ingredient functions, proportions, techniques, and transformations rather than only as a sequence of instructions.
zettels.body:
Understanding a recipe through structure means identifying why the preparation works. This includes recognizing the central ingredient relationships, the function of each component, the purpose of each technique, and the transformations expected during cooking.

Two recipes may appear different while sharing the same underlying structure. Their flavors or ingredients may change, but the proportional relationships and technical processes may remain similar.

Recognizing these patterns makes it easier to adapt recipes, troubleshoot failures, scale quantities, create variations, and develop original preparations. It also helps separate essential instructions from choices that can be modified.

This approach does not remove the need for recipes. It makes recipes more understandable by revealing the logic beneath their measurements and steps.
questions: What is the underlying structure of the recipe?
Which ingredients are essential to that structure?
What purpose does each step serve?
Which parts can be changed without breaking the preparation?
What does the recipe share with similar preparations?

zettels.title: Food Yields
zettels.mainIdea: Food yield is the usable amount of an ingredient remaining after trimming, preparation, cooking, and other forms of loss.
zettels.body:
The purchased weight or volume of an ingredient is not always the quantity available for serving or recipe production. Peeling, trimming, deboning, cleaning, cooking, draining, and portioning can reduce the usable amount.

Food-yield information connects the quantity purchased with the quantity that can actually be used. Understanding this relationship supports accurate purchasing, recipe costing, production planning, portioning, and waste control.

Yield varies according to ingredient quality, condition, size, season, preparation standards, employee technique, equipment, and cooking method. Published yield information provides a useful reference, but an operation should also conduct its own tests when accuracy is important.
questions: What quantity was purchased?
What usable quantity remained?
Where did the product loss occur?
Does the reference yield match the actual kitchen yield?
How does the yield affect purchasing and cost?

zettels.title: As-Purchased Quantity
zettels.mainIdea: As-purchased quantity is the full amount of an ingredient obtained before trimming, cleaning, cooking, or other preparation losses occur.
zettels.body:
As-purchased quantity represents the weight, volume, count, or package amount received from a supplier. It includes both usable product and any parts that may later be removed or lost.

For example, the as-purchased weight of a whole vegetable includes peels, stems, roots, damaged portions, and other material that may not enter the final preparation. The as-purchased weight of meat may include bones, exterior fat, connective tissue, or packaging liquid.

The as-purchased quantity is used when ordering ingredients and calculating the original purchase cost. It must be distinguished from edible-portion quantity when determining how much product is needed for a recipe or service.
questions: In what unit was the ingredient purchased?
Does the purchased amount include unusable material?
What preparation losses are expected?
How much must be purchased to meet the edible-portion requirement?

zettels.title: Edible-Portion Quantity
zettels.mainIdea: Edible-portion quantity is the usable amount of an ingredient available after preparation losses have been remove
zettels.body:
Edible-portion quantity represents the amount that can enter a recipe, be cooked, or be served after unusable material has been removed. It may be measured by weight, volume, or count.

The difference between as-purchased quantity and edible-portion quantity may result from peeling, trimming, deboning, cleaning, draining, or discarding damaged material. Cooking losses may also be included when the required quantity is based on the finished cooked product.

Edible-portion quantity is essential for accurate recipe costing b
questions: What preparation occurred before measurement?
Is the edible portion measured raw or cooked?
How much usable product remains?
What is the true cost of the usable quantity?

zettels.title: Yield Percentage
zettels.mainIdea: Yield percentage expresses the usable portion of an ingredient as a percentage of its original as-purchased quantity.
zettels.body:
Yield percentage compares edible-portion quantity with as-purchased quantity. It shows how much of the purchased product remains usable after trimming, cleaning, fabrication, cooking, or other losses.

A higher yield percentage means that more of the purchased ingredient remains available for use. A lower yield percentage indicates greater loss, although a lower yield does not automatically mean the ingredient is a poor purchase. Product quality, purchase price, labor requirements, flavor, and the value of usable trim must also be considered.

Yield percentage can support purchasing calculations, cost comparisons, recipe costing, waste analysis, and production planning. Actual kitchen testing may be necessary because published percentages do not account for every product, supplier, or preparation standard.

Calculation

Yield Percentage = Edible-Portion Quantity ÷ As-Purchased Quantity × 100
questions: What was the as-purchased quantity?
What edible quantity remained?
Were both quantities measured in the same unit?
What caused the product loss?
Does the yield percentage remain consistent across tests?

zettels.title: Food-Cost Calculations
zettels.mainIdea: Food-cost calculations determine the financial value of ingredients, recipes, portions, and menu items using accurate purchase, yield, and usage information.
zettels.body:
Food cost begins with the price paid for an ingredient, but the purchase price does not always represent the cost of the usable product. Trimming, preparation, and cooking losses increase the effective cost of the edible portion.

Accurate calculations may include as-purchased cost, edible-portion cost, recipe ingredient cost, total recipe cost, cost per portion, and food-cost percentage. The calculation used depends on the decision being made.

Reliable food costing requires consistent units, current purchase prices, verified yields, accurate recipe quantities, and realistic portion sizes. Incorrect yield information or uncontrolled portions can cause the calculated cost to differ significantly from the actual operating cost.
questions: Is the cost based on the purchased or usable quantity?
Are current ingredient prices being used?
Have yield losses been included?
What is the cost per recipe and per portion?
How does the cost affect pricing and profitability?

zettels.title: Portion Control
zettels.mainIdea: Portion control establishes and maintains the intended quantity of food served to support consistency, cost management, production planning, and the dining experience.
zettels.body:
A portion is the defined amount of a preparation or ingredient intended for one serving. Portion control ensures that this quantity remains reasonably consistent across production and service.

Consistent portions support predictable food cost, nutritional calculation, plating, guest expectations, and purchasing. Uncontrolled portions may cause shortages, excess waste, inconsistent presentation, and inaccurate menu costs.

Portion control may use scales, scoops, ladles, measuring tools, standardized cuts, piece counts, or visual standards. The appropriate method depends on the ingredient, service style, required precision, and production environment.

The goal is not simply to reduce portions. It is to provide the quantity intended for the dish while maintaining quality, value, and consistency.
questions: What is the intended serving quantity?
How will the portion be measured consistently?
Does the portion support the intended plate and guest experience?
How does portion variation affect yield and cost?

zettels.title: Purchasing Quantities
zettels.mainIdea: Purchasing quantities are determined by the usable product required, expected yield, production needs, existing inventory, and anticipated demand
zettels.body:
The amount that must be purchased is not always equal to the amount required by the recipe. When an ingredient loses weight or volume during cleaning, trimming, fabrication, or cooking, additional product must be purchased to provide the required usable quantity.

Purchasing calculations should consider expected yield, portion size, number of servings, existing inventory, supplier packaging, storage capacity, shelf life, and anticipated waste.

Ordering too little may interrupt production or reduce serving quantities. Ordering too much may increase spoilage, storage pressure, and unnecessary spending. Accurate purchasing connects menu planning, forecasting, recipes, yields, inventory, and supplier information.
questions: How much edible product is required?
What yield percentage should be expected?
What quantity is already in inventory?
How is the product packaged and sold?
What amount can be stored and used before spoilage?

zettels.title: Ingredient Waste
zettels.mainIdea: Ingredient waste is product that is purchased but does not become part of the intended usable preparation or service.
zettels.body:
Ingredient waste can occur during receiving, storage, trimming, preparation, cooking, portioning, and service. Some loss is unavoidable, such as inedible peels, bones, shells, or moisture evaporation. Other losses may result from poor handling, overproduction, spoilage, incorrect storage, inconsistent trimming, cooking errors, or excessive portions.

Not all trim should automatically be classified as waste. Some parts may be used in stocks, sauces, garnishes, staff meals, secondary preparations, preservation, or other applications when safe and appropriate.

Waste records can help identify whether losses are expected or preventable. Understanding the source of waste supports more accurate purchasing, costing, training, menu development, and sustainable kitchen practices.
questions: At what stage did the loss occur?
Was the loss necessary or preventable?
Can the trim be safely repurposed?
Does the actual loss match the expected yield?
What process change could reduce unnecessary waste?

zettels.title: Recipe Costing
zettels.mainIdea: Recipe costing calculates the total ingredient cost of a standardized recipe and the cost of each portion it produces.
zettels.body:
Recipe costing assigns a monetary value to every ingredient quantity used in a recipe. The calculation should use the cost of the actual usable amount, including yield losses when ingredients are purchased in a form different from the form used in the recipe.

The total recipe cost is determined by adding the cost of each ingredient. Dividing that total by the verified recipe yield provides the cost per portion or unit.

Accurate recipe costing depends on current purchase prices, consistent measurement units, standardized recipes, reliable yields, and controlled portions. Additional operating expenses may be considered during menu pricing, but they should not be confused with the direct ingredient cost of the recipe.
questions: What is the usable cost of each ingredient?
What is the verified recipe yield?
What is the cost per portion?
Are the prices and yields current?
Does the standardized portion match the costing calculation?

zettels.title: Product-Yield Testing
zettels.mainIdea: Product-yield testing measures the actual quantity and cost changes that occur as an ingredient moves from its purchased form to its usable or cooked form.
zettels.body:
A product-yield test begins by recording the ingredient’s as-purchased weight, count, volume, and cost. The ingredient is then cleaned, trimmed, fabricated, cooked, or otherwise prepared according to the operation’s normal method.

The usable product and any waste or trim are measured separately. These measurements make it possible to calculate yield percentage, cost per usable unit, and the quantity that must be purchased for production.

Testing should use consistent procedures, accurate scales, clearly defined trim standards, and representative products. Multiple tests may be needed because ingredient size, quality, condition, season, supplier, and employee technique can affect the result.

The purpose is to establish a realistic operational yield rather than depend entirely on a general reference value.
questions: What was the original purchased quantity and cost?
What preparation method was used?
How much edible product remained?
How much trim or waste was produced?
Does the result differ from the published reference yield?
Should the test be repeated for accuracy?

zettels.title: Access Shapes Culinary Learning
zettels.mainIdea: While reading Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat, I sometimes felt that the book was biased or dismissive toward people whose path into culinary knowledge included culinary school. This may not have been Samin Nosrat’s intention, but her opportunities to travel and learn through direct culinary experiences were different from the opportunities available to me.
zettels.body:
While reading Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat, there were points where I felt that the book was biased or dismissive toward people who attended culinary school.

I do not know whether this was Samin Nosrat’s intention. My response comes from the difference between the path she describes and the path I had to take.

She was able to travel, work in different culinary environments, learn from chefs, and gain knowledge through direct experience without having to attend culinary school. I did not have access to the same opportunities or the money required to follow that kind of path.

For me, culinary school was not unnecessary. It was part of how I gained access to culinary knowledge, structure, training, and experience. I attended school because that was the path available to me.

Because of that difference, some parts of the book felt as though the path of those who needed culinary school was being undervalued or dismissed. The book may not have intended to communicate that, but that is how certain parts affected me as a reader and culinary graduate.

This response does not mean that I reject the book or the knowledge it contains. I still use it as a reference and continue reading it. However, I also need to remain aware of how a writer’s opportunities and experiences shape the way culinary knowledge is presented.

My experience may cause me to receive that presentation differently because I had to gain my education through another path.

Passage That Prompted This Reflection

[Insert the exact passage from the book here.]

My Response

This passage made me feel that the path of people who attended culinary school was being dismissed or undervalued. I cannot say with certainty that this was Samin Nosrat’s intention, but her path included opportunities to travel and learn directly through professional culinary environments without having to attend culinary school.

My path was different. I did not have the same opportunities or financial access, and culinary school was part of how I gained structured knowledge, training, experience, and credentials. Because of that difference, I received this passage differently.

  • Passage That Prompted the Reflection
    Add the exact passage, page number, and chapter or section.

  • My Response
    Explain what the passage made you feel.

  • Why I Responded That Way
    Connect it to your own path through culinary school and the opportunities you did or did not have.

  • My Interpretation
    Separate what the passage actually says from what you think it may imply.

  • Questions Raised
    Keep the questions that can lead to later study or writing.
questions: Was the book dismissing culinary school, or was I responding to the difference between her opportunities and mine?
How did Samin Nosrat’s access to travel and direct culinary experience shape the way she presented learning?
How has my culinary-school experience shaped the way I read this book?
Can I value the knowledge in the book while still questioning parts of its perspective?
What different paths do people take to gain culinary knowledge?
What do I need this information to do?

zettels.title: Growing Crops in Food Deserts
zettels.mainIdea: Community growing spaces could increase access to fresh food in food deserts by producing crops within or near the communities that need them.
zettels.body:
Growing crops in food deserts could connect sustainability, food access, community participation, and culinary knowledge.

Community gardens, rooftop gardens, indoor growing systems, vacant lots, and other available spaces could be used to produce food closer to where people live. The purpose would not only be to create green spaces but to increase access to fresh ingredients in communities where that access is limited.

The crops grown should be connected to what the community actually eats. Culinary knowledge can help determine which vegetables, herbs, fruits, and other crops would be useful, culturally relevant, adaptable to local growing conditions, and capable of supporting affordable meals.

The system could also include education about preparing, preserving, and using the harvest. Surplus crops could be distributed, sold affordably, preserved, or connected to a community grocery store.

This idea connects food production with what happens after harvest. Growing food alone does not guarantee access. Distribution, affordability, culinary knowledge, storage, preservation, and community participation must also be considered.

Potential Agricultural Connection

One place I already have in mind is The Chef’s Garden in Huron, Ohio. I met Farmer Lee Jones while I was attending culinary school.

His work and the farm’s connection between agriculture, chefs, specialty crops, sustainability, and culinary education make them relevant to this idea. I may want to study their model further or eventually explore whether they could offer knowledge, guidance, sourcing, collaboration, or another form of connection.

At this stage, this is a possible direction to investigate, not an established partnership.
futureUse: potential partnership or consultation with Farmer Lee Jones and The Chef’s Garden, additional local farm partnerships
questions: What crops would be most useful to the community?
What growing spaces are available?
Who would own, manage, and maintain the growing spaces?
How would the food reach residents?
How could culinary knowledge support the use of the harvest?
How would the project remain affordable and sustainable?
What do I need this information to do?
What type of relationship would I want to explore with Farmer Lee Jones or The Chef’s Garden?
Would the connection involve sourcing, agricultural guidance, education, crop planning, surplus produce, or another form of collaboration?
What should I research before approaching them?

zettels.title: Grocery Access Through Imperfect and Surplus Food
zettels.mainIdea: A grocery store focused primarily on cosmetically imperfect, surplus, and overlooked food could reduce waste while providing more affordable food in communities with limited grocery access.
zettels.body:
I see the possibility of creating a grocery store that focuses primarily on food often described as ugly, imperfect, surplus, or unwanted by conventional retailers.

The food may be rejected because of appearance, size, shape, excess inventory, packaging changes, short remaining shelf life, or other reasons that do not necessarily make it unusable.

The purpose would not simply be to sell rejected food. The store would connect food-waste reduction with affordability and access, especially in communities that do not have reliable access to full grocery stores or fresh ingredients.

This concept could also connect with community growing projects. Crops produced by local gardens or urban farms could be sold or distributed through the store. The store could provide a market for usable surplus while giving residents access to produce, pantry goods, and other groceries.

My culinary background could shape how the store handles and communicates the food. This could include guidance on preparation, preservation, substitutions, storage, using unfamiliar ingredients, and turning imperfect products into complete meals.

The business would need to avoid treating communities as places where unwanted food can simply be deposited. The products must remain safe, useful, affordable, and connected to what residents actually need and eat.

Potential Local Farm Relationship

The Chef’s Garden in Huron, Ohio is one possible farm connection to consider. I met Farmer Lee Jones while attending culinary school, and I am familiar with the farm’s connection to chefs, specialty produce, sustainability, and culinary education.

I would need to determine whether its products, practices, knowledge, surplus crops, or professional network could have a role in this business concept. The purpose would not be to assume that the farm produces unwanted food or has agreed to supply the store. It would be to identify a real agricultural relationship that may be worth researching and respectfully exploring.
questions: Where would the store obtain imperfect and surplus food?
Would the store be physical, online, mobile, or a combination?
How would prices remain affordable while supporting the business?
How would food safety and remaining shelf life be managed?
What products would the community actually need?
How would the store differ from Misfits Market and similar companies?
Could locally grown crops be sold through the store?
How would the store avoid presenting the community as a destination for unwanted food?
What do I need this information to do?Could The Chef’s Garden contribute through sourcing, guidance, education, introductions, or crop planning?
Would its chef-focused production model align with a community grocery concept?
Could usable surplus, cosmetically imperfect produce, or secondary crop parts become part of the sourcing discussion?
How should I approach the farm without assuming its interest or availability?

zettels.title: Connecting Community Food Production and Grocery Access
zettels.mainIdea: Community growing projects and an imperfect-food grocery store could operate as connected parts of a local food system rather than as separate solutions.
zettels.body:
The community-growing idea and the grocery-store idea are connected.

Gardens and urban growing spaces could produce fresh crops locally. The grocery store could provide a consistent place to distribute or sell those crops while also sourcing cosmetically imperfect and surplus food from farms, distributors, producers, and other suppliers.

The grocery store could support the gardens by creating a market for their harvest. The gardens could support the store by providing locally grown, culturally relevant, and seasonal ingredients.

Culinary education could connect both parts of the system. Residents could receive information about preparing unfamiliar produce, storing ingredients, preserving seasonal harvests, reducing household waste, and creating affordable meals.

Organic material from the store and gardens might also support composting when safe and appropriate, returning some material to food production rather than sending it directly into the waste stream.

This could become a community food system involving production, sourcing, distribution, culinary use, education, preservation, waste reduction, and local economic activity.

Existing Connection to Explore

Farmer Lee Jones and The Chef’s Garden represent a possible agricultural connection within this larger system. I met Farmer Lee while attending culinary school, so this possibility comes from an actual point of contact rather than from selecting a farm at random.

The Chef’s Garden’s relationship with chefs and its emphasis on agricultural quality, sustainability, soil, and culinary use may provide knowledge relevant to linking crop production with grocery access.

The exact role remains undecided. Possibilities might include consultation, sourcing, education, introductions to other growers, crop planning, or studying the farm’s model. These possibilities must be researched rather than assumed.
questions: How would food move through the complete system?
Which parts would be operated by the business and which by the community?
How could the gardens and store financially support one another?
How would local needs determine what is grown and stocked?
What partnerships would the system require?
What parts should begin first?
What do I need this information to do?
What could I reasonably ask Farmer Lee Jones or The Chef’s Garden to contribute?
What part of their model could apply to a community-centered food system?

What part of their model could apply to a community-centered food system?
Would smaller or more local farms also be needed for regular sourcing?
How could the project benefit a farm partner rather than only asking the farm to support the project?

zettels.title: How sustainable is artificial intelligence?
zettels.mainIdea: Artificial intelligence may offer useful tools and solutions, but I need to examine whether the energy, water, hardware, infrastructure, and other resources required to build and operate AI make its continued expansion environmentally sustainable.
zettels.body:
My concern is how sustainable artificial intelligence actually is, beginning with what is required to power it.

AI systems depend on data centers, electricity, computer hardware, cooling systems, network infrastructure, storage, maintenance, and continued equipment replacement. I want to understand the environmental effects associated with training AI models, operating them, storing information, and processing individual requests.

The concern is not limited to electricity. I also need to consider the water used for cooling, the materials and minerals required to manufacture computer hardware, the environmental effects of producing and transporting that equipment, and what happens when the hardware is replaced or discarded.

I want to understand where the energy used by AI infrastructure comes from and whether claims about renewable energy reflect the complete environmental cost. A company may power part of its operation with renewable electricity while still depending on resource extraction, manufacturing, water use, construction, transportation, and electronic waste.

AI may also be used to support sustainability through research, energy management, agriculture, climate modeling, waste reduction, transportation, and other applications. However, those possible benefits do not automatically make AI itself sustainable.

The question is whether the environmental benefits created through AI can justify or outweigh the resources consumed by the systems supporting it.

I also want to examine who receives the benefits of AI and who bears the environmental costs of its infrastructure. Data centers, energy production, water use, mineral extraction, manufacturing, and electronic waste may affect communities that do not receive equal benefits from the technology.

This note is not based on a conclusion that AI is sustainable or unsustainable. It establishes the questions I need to investigate before reaching a conclusion.
futureUse: essay on the environmental cost of AI
questions: How much energy is required to train AI models?
How much energy is required to operate AI after training?
How much water is used to cool AI data centers?
Where does the electricity powering AI infrastructure come from?
What resources are required to manufacture AI hardware?
How often must AI hardware be replaced?
What happens to discarded AI equipment?
How are AI-related emissions calculated and reported?
Do renewable-energy claims include the full environmental cost?
Can AI’s sustainability benefits outweigh its resource use?
Who benefits from AI and who bears its environmental costs?
What do I need this information to do?

zettels.title: The Title "Chef"
zettels.mainIdea: “Chef” is several things at once: a title, a position, a form of respect, and a call-and-response acknowledgment when orders or instructions are given
zettels.body:
The word “Chef” carries several meanings at the same time.

It is a title. It identifies someone as a chef and recognizes the role they hold.

It is a position. Within the structure of a kitchen, “Chef” can identify rank, responsibility, authority, and a person’s place in the operation.

It is also a form of respect. Addressing someone as “Chef” acknowledges the person and the role they hold.

During service, “Chef” can function as a call and response. When an order, instruction, correction, or direction is given, responding with “Chef” acknowledges that the speaker was heard and that the instruction was received.

The meaning of the word can change according to who says it, how it is said, and the situation in which it is used. It may communicate respect, acknowledgment, discipline, authority, responsibility, readiness, or understanding.

The title is therefore not only a name for a profession. It also functions within the language, hierarchy, rhythm, and culture of the kitchen.
futureUse: study of kitchen language and culture

What is the difference between earning the title Chef
being given the position

How does Chef function as a form of respect?
How does Chef identify position within the kitchen hierarchy?
How does Chef acknowledge an order
instruction
or correction?
How does Chef work as call and response during service?
How does tone change the meaning of Chef?
Does Chef identify authority
responsibility
service
discipline
or all of them at once?
How does Chef function differently inside and outside the kitchen?
