🧾 Ingredients

ImperialMetricIngredientPreparationTime1 bag, 1.5 lb680 gLittle Potato Company Little Yellows Fresh Creamer PotatoesWashed, drained, and halved if large5 minutes1 package, 10 oz284 gShredded Brussels sproutsInspected and separated2 minutes1/4 cup60 mLBrooklyn Delhi Golden Coconut Curry Simmer SauceStirred before measuring1 minute2 tablespoons30 mLOlive oilDivided1 minute1/4 cup20 gDehydrated onionRehydrated and drained10 minutes1/3 cup25 gDehydrated sweet pepperRehydrated and drained10 minutesTo tasteTo tasteSaltAdded gradually1 minuteTo tasteTo tasteBlack pepperFreshly ground if available1 minute

📖 Instructions

  1. Preheat a convection oven to 450°F (232°C). Position a rack in the center of the oven and line a large rimmed sheet pan with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

  2. Place the dehydrated onion and dehydrated sweet pepper in a heat-resistant bowl. Cover them with hot water and allow them to rehydrate for 10 minutes. Drain thoroughly and press out excess water.

  3. Wash and inspect the creamer potatoes. Halve any potatoes that are larger than approximately 1 inch (2.5 cm) in diameter so the pieces cook evenly.

  4. Place the potatoes in a microwave-safe covered container with 2 tablespoons (30 mL) water. Microwave for 5 to 7 minutes, or until slightly tender but not fully cooked. Drain well. Alternatively, simmer them in water for 8 to 10 minutes and drain thoroughly.

  5. Combine the par-cooked potatoes, shredded Brussels sprouts, rehydrated onion, rehydrated sweet pepper, olive oil, salt, and black pepper in a large mixing bowl.

  6. Add the Golden Coconut Curry Simmer Sauce and toss until the vegetables are evenly coated.

  7. Spread the mixture across the prepared sheet pan in a shallow, even layer. Turn the potatoes cut-side down and avoid overcrowding the Brussels sprouts.

  8. Roast at 450°F (232°C) on convection for 15 minutes.

  9. Remove the pan from the oven and turn the potatoes and Brussels sprouts with a flexible spatula. Redistribute any vegetables that are browning more quickly around the edges.

  10. Return the pan to the oven and roast for an additional 12 to 15 minutes, until the potatoes are tender, the Brussels sprouts have crisp caramelized edges, and the sauce is concentrated around the vegetables.

  11. Confirm that the center of the dish has reached at least 165°F (74°C). Remove the sheet pan from the oven.

  12. Taste and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper as needed.

  13. Allow the vegetables to rest on the sheet pan for 5 minutes so the curry coating thickens slightly and adheres to the vegetables.

  14. Transfer to a warmed serving platter or portion directly onto individual plates. Serve immediately.

🍽️ Plating:

Arrange the potatoes through the center of a shallow warmed bowl and mound the roasted Brussels sprouts over and around them. Spoon any concentrated curry mixture from the sheet pan over the vegetables. Finish with freshly ground black pepper. For added color, garnish with fresh cilantro or thinly sliced scallions when available.

📝 Notes

  • Par-cooking the potatoes helps them become creamy inside during the same roasting time required to caramelize the shredded Brussels sprouts.

  • Drain the rehydrated onion and peppers thoroughly. Excess water can steam the vegetables and reduce browning.

  • Use a sufficiently large sheet pan. Overcrowding traps moisture and produces softer vegetables.

  • The curry sauce contains coconut cream, ginger, turmeric, lemon, onion, garlic, and spices, giving the dish richness and mild aromatic heat.

  • The nutritional estimate assumes six servings and approximately 1 teaspoon of added salt for the complete recipe.

  • The stated ingredient cost is approximately $15.98 before accounting for salt, pepper, and any delivery charges.

🧊 Storage:

Cool leftovers promptly in shallow containers. Refrigerate at 41°F (5°C) or below for up to 4 days. Reheat uncovered in a 400°F (204°C) convection oven for 8 to 12 minutes, or until the center reaches 165°F (74°C). The dish may be frozen for up to 2 months, although the Brussels sprouts and potatoes may soften after thawing.

How sustainable is artificial intelligence?

AI requires energy to power data centers, train models, process requests, store information, and operate the infrastructure supporting it. I want to understand where that energy comes from, how much is required, and what environmental effects result from the growing use of AI.

The concern is not limited to electricity. AI may also require water for cooling data centers, physical land and buildings, computer hardware, minerals, manufacturing, transportation, maintenance, and the replacement or disposal of equipment.

I want to examine whether the benefits and uses of AI justify the resources it consumes, how its environmental impact is measured, and whether companies are accurately reporting that impact.

I also want to study whether AI can contribute to sustainability while simultaneously creating its own sustainability problems. The question is not simply whether AI is useful, but whether the systems supporting it can continue expanding without causing unacceptable environmental and resource costs.

fleetingNotes.topic: I Built the Dungeon That Killed Me
fleetingNotes.rawCapture: The book title "I Built the Dungeon That Killed Me" inspired an idea for a poem. The central premise is that the speaker has constructed the very thing that ultimately confines or destroys them. The dungeon is built gradually, through choices, habits, actions, or repeated acts whose consequences may not be understood while they are happening. A central tension is: if I built the dungeon myself, why can't I leave it? The poem could allow that question to remain unanswered.
notes: Preserve the idea of construction happening over time: stone follows stone, choice follows choice.

Keep the dungeon concrete rather than metaphorically ornate: doors, locks, walls, keys, mortar, rooms.
Emotion should emerge through accumulation rather than explanation.
Possible themes include self-sabotage, grief, addiction, ambition, isolation, guilt, identity, or remaining inside a relationship after its emotional life has ended.
Do not decide the final meaning before drafting. Let the dungeon acquire its meaning through the poem.
Core unresolved question: If I built it, why can't I leave it?

sources.title: Tilly Norwood’s New Movie Rekindles Hollywood Concerns That AI “Actor” Is Just Ripping Off Human Performances
sources.author: Corbin Bolies
sources.copiedText:
Tilly Norwood’s New Movie Rekindles Hollywood Concerns That AI ‘Actor’ Is Just Ripping Off Human Performances

Particle6 TV

The news of Tilly Norwood’s feature-length movie debut again brought out the digital pitchforks surrounding her existence, with commenters weighing in on everything from the concept of an AI actress leading a film to why entertainment outlets such as Variety covered the news. 

Norwood’s creator is taking the backlash in stride, insisting that she’s just trying to show the industry the art of what’s possible with the tech.

AI-focused studio Particle 6 announced Monday that it was in production on “Misaligned,” a comedy-drama Norwood will “star” in that will combine human crewmembers with AI tools.

Eline van der Velden, founder and CEO of the London-based company, told Variety via email that the intention behind the feature is to “demonstrate where AI is at — and upskill and bring as many people as possible from the industry with us into the future.”

“More people than ever before are hearing and understanding that message,” she said, claiming there’s been a “noticeable uplift” in interest from creatives since the announcement. “And if we can get more people working in AI and future-proofing their roles, a little criticism won’t matter.”

Whether people in the entertainment industry really are receptive to that message is open for debate. Many of the associations representing professionals in the biz showed little desire to discuss Norwood’s film debut. But what’s clear is that some in Hollywood see the Norwood persona as a persistent threat and continue to question whether the AI “actor” has been trained on content without permission or compensation.

In a statement to Variety, U.K. performers’ union Equity said that when “it comes to the use of AI avatars — whether that’s ‘Tilly Norwood’ or any others — there are concerns about how a digital replica or avatar was created” and that it believed “transparency, consent and remuneration are key to addressing AI use in the film, TV and audio industries.”

“While data scraping and untraceable training data sources continue, the questions of theft and misuse will persist,” Cathy Sweet, Equity’s head of film and TV, said in a statement. “Actors, voice artists and performers of all kinds are left vulnerable to their work being stolen and used without their consent or even knowledge. This isn’t OK and it has to stop.”

Because Norwood is not a person, she “can’t really be a performer,” said Ted Tremper, interim executive director of the Creators Coalition on AI whose co-founders include the Daniels, Natasha Lyonne and former Academy president Janet Yang.

“It’s a character that’s created from that’s an assemblage of a tremendous amount of unseen extracted creativity and the name, image, and likenesses of people who haven’t been credited or compensated for the work that it took to create,” Tremper said, adding that she posed the question of “whether or not people know how it’s made and whether or not the human beings whose work was extracted to create it are being respected and paid.”

Representatives for the Writers Guild of America and the Directors Guild of America, two unions representing Hollywood’s legion of scribes and filmmakers, did not respond to Variety’s requests for comment on the news about a Norwood-led film. The Motion Pictures Editors Guild declined to comment for now about the prospect of editors working on a film featuring Norwood, while the Hollywood performers’ union, SAG-AFTRA, pointed to its past statements on Norwood’s emergence, one of which called her the “synthetic construct generated by software trained on the work of countless professional performers, real human beings, whose work was taken without permission, without credit and without compensation.”

According to van der Velden, Norwood was not “based on any specific person’s likeness” and instead created through “original prompting, thousands of iterations and substantial human creative oversight” along with “openly available tools — which draw on everything ever uploaded to the internet — including my own work as an actress.” Norwood will only appear in films created by AI, she said, not those featuring real people.

“Yes, we agree, Tilly isn’t a person,” van der Velden added. “She is an AI actor, a character created by Particle 6 to highlight, demonstrate and teach people about AI.”

Nearly a year after Norwood broke into public view with van der Velden’s claim that talent agencies were eager to represent the AI performer, one talent agency partner told Variety they couldn’t “imagine the complexities of representing a synthetic actor like a Tilly, given that that’s not a person.” Agencies including WME and Gersh also have bucked at the thought. Van der Velden said Particle 6’s conversations with talent agencies ceased after September and the company doesn’t believe one is necessary at the moment.

Tremper said he could imagine a future where AI usage isn’t vilified and synthetic or duplicated actors emerge with proper compensation. However, he said, doing so would require “a tremendous amount of good faith” collaboration between those making and using the technology.

“Once we actually, as a society, understand the ways that things are made, we are able to form a consensus,” he said, such as through voting or community organizing. “I think the most insidious thing that happens is that the people who make these [AI] tools, services and characters want to convince the audience that they don’t have a choice or that they don’t have self-determination, and that all of this is inevitable, and that is extraordinary. That is demonstrably false.”

The tug-of-war surrounding Norwood’s existence comes as the industry continues to grapple with generative AI. Reactions in the business have ranged from ostracization to tepid curiosity — and all the way to wholesale embrace, all while studios try to enforce regulations that protect humans’ likenesses and jobs.

Illumination CEO Chris Meledandri, speaking to Variety at the “Minions & Monsters” premiere just before word of Norwood’s feature-film debut came out, said his team was “complete believers in the human imagination” and felt “no pressure to push AI into our pipeline.”

“I wish I had a crystal ball,” Meledandri added. “I wish I could understand where it’s going, and I worry about the future of work across all industries.”

Marc Malkin contributed to this report.
sources.summary: The article discusses renewed concerns surrounding Tilly Norwood, an AI-generated actor created by Eline Van der Velden’s company, Particle6. The article places the project within the wider debate over artificial intelligence, creative work, performers’ rights, and the future use of AI-generated actors in filmmaking.

sources.title: Mount Gay Rum
sources.author: Mount Gay Distilleries Ltd.
sources.copiedText:
Mount Gay presents Barbados and its rum-making tradition as inseparable, shaped by the island’s geology, culture, landscape, and centuries of craftsmanship.

Water
Mount Gay uses water from a deep artesian well located on its original property in Saint Lucy, Barbados. The well was first dug in 1703 and remains in use. The water rises from coral caverns hundreds of feet underground and is naturally filtered through the island’s coral geology.

Yeast and Fermentation
Yeast converts the sugars in molasses into alcohol during fermentation. Mount Gay uses two fermentation methods.

Closed fermentation is used for column distillation and uses a proprietary heirloom yeast strain developed by Mount Gay’s rum makers.

Open-air fermentation is used for pot-still distillation. The molasses-and-water mixture is exposed to the Barbadian environment, allowing native airborne yeasts to enter the fermentation and contribute to the rum’s aromatic character.

Molasses
Mount Gay uses molasses produced from selected Barbadian and Caribbean sugarcane. The molasses has a malty character with notes of caramel and toffee, along with acidity and slight bitterness in the finish.

Key Significance
The character of Mount Gay rum is connected to Barbados through its water, native yeasts, sugarcane, climate, geology, and traditional production methods.
sources.summary: Official Mount Gay Rum website featuring the company’s rum collections, cocktail recipes, rum-making process, Barbadian heritage, distillery tours, visitor experiences, news, events, and product information. The website identifies Barbados as the birthplace of rum and presents Mount Gay as operating since 1703.

The book connects professional culinary principles with practical home cooking and encourages cooks to observe, taste, understand, and adjust food throughout the cooking process. Wendy MacNaughton provided the book’s illustrations.

sources.author: Karen Page, Andrew Dornenburg
sources.summary:
The Flavor Bible is a culinary reference guide centered on flavor relationships, ingredient affinities, and creative decision-making. Rather than functioning primarily as a conventional recipe book, it organizes ingredients and identifies flavors, seasonings, techniques, and other ingredients that experienced chefs associate with them.

The book supports cooks in developing dishes by understanding how flavors relate, identifying complementary and contrasting combinations, and making informed choices based on season, taste, aroma, texture, temperature, and culinary intention. It presents flavor pairing as a foundation for culinary creativity rather than as a fixed set of formulas. The original edition was published in 2008 by Little, Brown and Company.

sources.title: The Flavor Matrix: The Art and Science of Pairing Common Ingredients to Create Extraordinary Dishes
sources.author: James Briscione, Brooke Parkhurst
sources.summary:
The Flavor Matrix is a culinary reference and flavor-pairing guide that connects ingredient combinations with shared aromatic compounds. It uses visual matrices and ingredient groupings to show how common ingredients may pair with complementary foods, seasonings, and flavors.

The book combines food science with culinary creativity, helping cooks explore relationships between aroma, taste, and ingredients when developing dishes. It can support both familiar combinations and less obvious pairings by providing a structured starting point for experimentation rather than a fixed formula for what must be combined. The book was published in 2018 and includes original recipes demonstrating its flavor-pairing approach.flavor matrix, flavor development, flavor pairing, aromatic compounds, ingredient affinities, food science, culinary creativity, intuitive cooking, recipe development, ingredient reference

sources.title: Ratio: The Simple Codes Behind the Craft of Everyday Cooking
sources.author: Michael Ruhlman
sources.summary:
Ratio presents foundational cooking preparations through proportional relationships between ingredients. Michael Ruhlman explains how understanding ratios can help cooks recognize the underlying structure of doughs, batters, custards, stocks, sauces, and other preparations.

The book emphasizes learning how ingredients function together rather than depending only on fixed recipes. By understanding the relationship between quantities, a cook can scale preparations, make substitutions, develop variations, troubleshoot results, and create new recipes with greater control. The book contains thirty-three culinary ratios and examples of how changing a ratio can transform one preparation into another.

sources.title: The Book of Yields: Accuracy in Food Costing and Purchasing
sources.author: Francis T. Lynch
sources.summary:
The Book of Yields is a culinary and hospitality reference for calculating usable food quantities, purchasing requirements, portions, recipe costs, and ingredient yields. It provides yield information for raw ingredients and helps cooks determine how much usable product remains after trimming, peeling, deboning, cooking, or other preparation.

The book supports purchasing and production decisions by connecting as-purchased quantity, edible-portion quantity, yield percentage, portion size, and cost. It can be used to estimate ordering quantities, reduce waste, calculate more accurate recipe costs, establish portions, and test actual ingredient yields within a kitchen operation.

sources.title: Emperor’s Earth
sources.author: Darrell Pender
sources.summary:
Emperor’s Earth is a speculative-fiction manuscript centered on Kido Thompson after a Mirrian attack destroys much of Earth’s population. Kido survives and develops extraordinary abilities that place him between the possibility of becoming a protector and leader or becoming SHIVA, the destroyer of worlds.

The manuscript follows Kido’s relationships with Ricky Chapman, Kenji Nakamura, Mira Devereaux, Xavier, Ja-Jorel, and others as he struggles with trauma, responsibility, power, identity, manipulation, and rebuilding. Doctor Henry Feldman attempts to study, control, program, and use Kido through genetic research, behavioral manipulation, and ancient technology.

The story also involves The Order, the Russian Federation, Colonel Reed Hawkes, the Mirrians, political and military power, covert experimentation, alien contact, survival, reconciliation, and the ethical consequences of power. The manuscript includes twelve chapters, character profiles, organization profiles, Mirrian terminology, a working Mirrinese lexicon, and Kido’s notes concerning what Earth must build going forward.

sources.title: I, Robot
sources.author: Isaac Asimov
sources.archiveLocation: Personal library, Kindle library, Audiobook library
sources.summary:
I, Robot is a collection of interconnected science-fiction stories examining robots, human behavior, artificial intelligence, and the consequences of programming machines to obey fixed rules.

The stories are connected through the recollections of robopsychologist Susan Calvin and explore situations involving the Three Laws of Robotics. Rather than presenting the laws as simple solutions, the stories examine conflicts caused by interpretation, competing instructions, incomplete information, human motives, and unforeseen consequences.

The book uses robot behavior to investigate questions of obedience, safety, responsibility, logic, morality, and humanity’s attempts to control intelligent systems.

sources.copiedText: A distinctive, earthy, usually pleasant odor that is associated with rainfall.”
sources.summary:
Defines petrichor as the earthy odor associated with rainfall, particularly when rain follows warm, dry weather. The entry identifies volatile plant oils, geosmin released from soil, and ozone as possible contributors to the broader smell.

sources.title: Aerosol Generation by Raindrop Impact on Soil

sources.title: The New Cocktail Hour: The Essential Guide to Handcrafted Drinks (Revised & Expanded Edition)
sources.author: André Darlington; Tenaya Darlington
sources.copiedText:
So what is a craft cocktail exactly? It’s a mixed drink in which all the elements—from spirits to mixers to garnishes—have been selected with care to create visual appeal, seductive aroma, balanced taste, depth of flavor, appropriate mouthfeel, and above all, pizzazz. The great ones even have a good story. Like a bespoke suit or a handmade bag, the final product transcends the ordinary. It sings. It embodies inspiration, quality, and skill. Does this mean you need to begin an in-home ice program and invest in a sous vide appliance? No. With a little creativity and a few tips, you can craft fine drinks at home without a lot of fuss or special equipment.

Page 13.
sources.summary: A reference work on handcrafted cocktails that explains cocktail construction, ingredients, techniques, balance, presentation, and the principles that distinguish a carefully crafted drink from an ordinary mixed drink.

sources.title: Prepare for Death and Follow Me — Traditional Memento Mori Epitaph
sources.author: Traditional / Unknown
sources.copiedText:
Remember me as you pass by.

As you are now, so once was I.

As I am now, so you must be.

Prepare for death and follow me.
sources.summary:
Traditional funerary epitaph appearing in numerous variations on gravestones in Britain, Ireland, and the United States.

The verse addresses the living from the perspective of the dead: the deceased was once as the reader is now, and the reader will eventually share the deceased's condition. It functions as a memento mori—a reminder of mortality and the inevitability of death.

Versions of the epitaph appear extensively in historic American cemeteries, including colonial and nineteenth-century New England, while related forms also occur in British and Irish churchyards.

Its underlying idea is substantially older than any single surviving gravestone and belongs to a broader tradition of the dead warning or addressing the living.

sources.title: Tiny Garden Habit-Brush These 5 Herbs for a Burst of Fragrance
sources.author: Tiny Garden Habit
sources.copiedText:
BRUSH THESE 5 HERBS FOR A BURST OF FRAGRANCE

A light rub can release more of their natural aroma.

MINT
Fresh, cool

LEMON BALM
Lemony

ROSEMARY
Piney

THYME
Warm, herbal

BASIL
Sweet, spicy

👋 A gentle rub or pinch releases the aromatic oils in leaves like mint, rosemary, thyme, and basil.

🚶 I like putting thyme or rosemary near paths so the fragrance gets released as I work around them.

🪴 Mint and lemon balm can spread aggressively, so I usually keep them contained rather than giving them free run of a bed.

☀️ Rosemary and thyme smell strongest for me when they’re growing in plenty of sun and well-drained soil.

🌱 Basil is much more tender, so I keep harvesting the tips while the weather is warm to encourage fresh leafy growth.
sources.summary:
Tiny Garden Habit shared a branded Facebook infographic identifying mint, lemon balm, rosemary, thyme, and basil as aromatic herbs whose fragrance becomes more noticeable when their foliage is lightly rubbed or disturbed. The accompanying Facebook text expands on the infographic by discussing the placement of rosemary and thyme near paths, containment of spreading mint and lemon balm, sunny and well-drained growing conditions for rosemary and thyme, and regular harvesting of basil tips during warm weather to encourage fresh leafy growth.

The post was published directly on the Tiny Garden Habit Facebook page. No external article or website link accompanied the post.

sources.title: Christian Nationalism, War Machine, AIPAC, and Broligarchy
sources.author: ChatGPT
sources.copiedText:
Christian nationalists are people who believe that Christianity should have a special or defining role in the identity, government, laws, or culture of their nation. In the United States, the term usually refers to the belief that America is fundamentally a Christian nation and should be governed in a way that reflects that identity.

It is important to separate Christianity, patriotism, and Christian nationalism. A Christian can love their country, vote according to their religious convictions, advocate for policies, or want Christian moral ideas represented in public life without necessarily being a Christian nationalist. Christian nationalism goes further by connecting national belonging and political authority with Christianity itself.

Stronger forms of Christian nationalism may include beliefs such as:

Being Christian is an important part of being a “real” American.

Political leaders should share Christian beliefs.

Biblical teachings should substantially influence American law.

Christianity should receive a privileged position compared with other religions.

In its strongest form, biblical authority should take precedence over the preferences expressed through democratic government.

There is a spectrum. Some supporters mean America should continue to be influenced by Christian moral traditions. Others mean America should explicitly be a Christian nation whose government and laws favor Christian teachings.

Critics argue that Christian nationalism can conflict with religious freedom and pluralistic democracy when it treats Christians as more authentically American than citizens belonging to other religions or no religion. Supporters may instead describe their position as preserving America's Christian heritage, traditional morality, or the right of Christians to participate openly in politics.

Christian: My faith influences how I live and how I vote.

Christian patriot: I am Christian and I love my country.

Christian nationalist: Christianity should be an important part of what defines this country and how it is governed.

The phrase “war machine” usually means the large system that enables a country to prepare for, conduct, and sustain war. It is not normally the name of one organization.

In American political discussion, it is often shorthand for the military-industrial complex: the interconnected relationship among the armed forces, government, defense contractors, weapons manufacturers, and the political and economic interests surrounding military spending.

This can include the military, Department of Defense, defense contractors, government contracts, Congress, lobbyists, research institutions, technology companies, and logistical, intelligence, financial, and industrial systems supporting military operations.

Government funding → military requirements → defense contracts → weapons production → military capability → continued funding.

Critics use “war machine” when arguing that this system can create economic or political incentives for high military spending or continued military involvement.

President Dwight D. Eisenhower warned about the influence of the “military-industrial complex” in his January 17, 1961 farewell address.

Calling something a war machine does not necessarily mean alleging a conspiracy. Separate institutions may have interests that reinforce one another without secret coordination.

Military = the armed forces.

Military-industrial complex = the military + defense industry + political/economic relationships surrounding them.

War machine = an informal and usually critical term for that larger system and its capacity to wage war.

AIPAC stands for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

AIPAC is a major pro-Israel advocacy and lobbying organization in the United States. Its stated mission is to strengthen the relationship between the United States and Israel by influencing U.S. policy and Congress.

Its work includes lobbying Congress concerning U.S. military and security assistance to Israel, missile-defense programs, Iran policy, and other U.S.–Israel matters.

It also participates in American elections through AIPAC PAC, while the AIPAC-backed United Democracy Project spends money supporting or opposing candidates.

AIPAC is an American organization rather than part of the Israeli government.

Its political influence operates through lobbying, campaign spending, political organization, donors, and relationships with lawmakers.

AIPAC can appear in discussions involving U.S. foreign policy, defense spending, support for Israel, lobbying, and some Christian evangelical political movements. These groups and systems may overlap in political coalitions but are not the same thing.

“Broligarchy” is a slang and usually critical term for a small group of extremely wealthy and powerful men, especially technology billionaires, who possess substantial political and economic influence.

The word combines “bro” and “oligarchy.”

An oligarchy is rule or control by a small privileged group. Broligarchy adds the idea that this group is dominated by wealthy male figures from technology, Silicon Valley, venture capital, or related industries.

The individuals are sometimes called “broligarchs.”

The term became more common in U.S. political discussion around the 2024 election and afterward, particularly in discussions of technology billionaires whose wealth, companies, political donations, media platforms, and government relationships can provide unusual influence.

Broligarchy is a political description or criticism, not the official name of an organization.

Christian nationalism → political ideology connecting Christianity and national identity/government.

War machine / military-industrial complex → network surrounding military power, government, and defense industry.

AIPAC → pro-Israel U.S. lobbying and political advocacy organization.

Broligarchy → alleged concentration of political and economic influence among wealthy male technology elites.

These concepts can overlap politically, but they are separate things.
sources.summary: Research conversation explaining four terms encountered in contemporary U.S. political discussion. Christian nationalism describes an ideology connecting Christianity with national identity and political authority and ranges from support for Christian cultural influence to support for formal governmental privilege for Christianity. “War machine” is an informal critical expression commonly associated with the military-industrial complex: the network connecting military institutions, government spending, defense industries, political actors, and other systems supporting warfare. AIPAC is the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a U.S. pro-Israel lobbying and political advocacy organization. “Broligarchy” is a critical political term describing the concentration of political and economic influence among extremely wealthy male technology elites. The concepts may intersect through political coalitions, lobbying, military policy, campaign spending, and concentrated power, but they should not be treated as interchangeable.

sources.summary:
CLEAR, IN-DEPTH INSTRUCTION ON CRITICAL COOKING THEORIES AND TECHNIQUES FOR CULINARY STUDENTS

The Tenth Edition of Professional Cooking reflects the changing nature of our understanding of cooking and related fields such as food safety, nutrition, and dietary practices, as well as the latest thinking about how best to teach this material. Chapters include relevant cultural and historical background for international recipes and cooking practices. What has not changed is the core material that focuses on the essentials ― the comprehensive understanding of ingredients and basic cooking techniques that are the foundation of success in the kitchen, and the development of fundamental skills to apply this knowledge.

NEW TO THIS EDITION

    Emphasis on special diets including vegetarian, keto, high protein, and more
    Two new appendices focused on kosher and halal ingredients and preparation
    All recipes throughout the book reviewed and freshened
    Vegan recipes now clearly labeled for ease of planning
    Simplified metric to imperial (US) comparison to facilitate common measurements
    Baking recipes updated for consistency with the latest edition of Professional Baking.
    Updated support material for instructors and students including PowerPoint slides, an Instructor’s Manual, Student Study Guide solutions, and test banks

AN INTERACTIVE, MULTIMEDIA LEARNING EXPERIENCE

This textbook includes access to an interactive, multimedia e-text. Icons throughout the print book signal corresponding digital content in the e-text.

    Interactive Figures and Content: Appearing throughout the enhanced e-text, interactive figures, visual learning activities, flashcards, and pop-up definitions facilitate the study of complex concepts and processes and help students retain important information. Even many of the simplest figures are interactive to encourage online readers to pause and absorb the information they present before scrolling on to additional reading.
    Interactive Practice Quizzes: Each chapter includes a self-scoring Practice Quiz to help prepare for graded assignments and exams.
    CulinarE-Companion Website:
        More than 200 videos demonstrating cooking techniques, culinary math concepts, and common kitchen procedures
        Enhanced tools to manage recipes or calculate nutritional analyses and food costing
        Audio pronunciation guides for more than 1000 glossary terms

sources.title: Professional Cooking
sources.author: Wayne Gisslen
sources.copiedText: HEAT AND FOOD — To cook food means to heat it in order to make certain changes in it. The section explains the theory of how foods behave when heated, including heat transfer and the physical and chemical reactions of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, water, minerals, vitamins, pigments, and flavor components.
sources.summary: Explains heat as molecular energy and describes how heating produces physical and chemical changes in food. Topics include caramelization, gelatinization, gelation, dextrinization, fiber softening, protein denaturation and coagulation, the Maillard reaction, connective tissue, fats and smoke points, nutrient and flavor loss, and the behavior of water during cooking.

He worked as a professional chef for more than 30 years and created ChefDesk.com as a resource for food-service professionals. His work focused on ingredient yields, purchasing, food costing, portioning, and kitchen production.
entities.roleUse: A culinary influence on my understanding of food yields, edible portions, purchasing quantities, ingredient waste, portion control, recipe costing, and accurate production planning.

entities.name: Misfits Market
entities.description: Online grocery company that sells produce, pantry items, and other groceries sourced partly through food-rescue and less-wasteful supply channels. The company describes its model as sourcing from farms and emerging producers while working toward a less wasteful food system. Misfits Market also operates alongside Imperfect Foods following their combination.
entities.roleUse:
• A company to research and compare with my concept for a community grocery store focused primarily on cosmetically imperfect, surplus, and overlooked food.

    The purpose of the comparison is not to reproduce its business model automatically. I need to examine what applies to my idea, what does not apply, and how my concept would differ by focusing on local communities, food deserts, physical grocery access, community-grown crops, culinary education, and culturally relevant food.

entities.name: Farmer Lee Jones
entities.description: Farmer Lee Jones is a farmer, agricultural advocate, and co-owner of The Chef’s Garden near Huron, Ohio. His work connects sustainable agriculture, soil health, specialty crop production, chefs, and culinary education.
entities.roleUse:
A person I met while attending culinary school and someone whose work may be relevant to my ideas about local farm partnerships, food access, community growing, culinary education, and a grocery store centered on imperfect, surplus, and locally grown food.

This record identifies a possible person to contact or learn from later. It does not mean that a partnership has been discussed or established.

entities.name: The Chef’s Garden
entities.description: Family farm near Huron, Ohio, known for growing specialty vegetables, herbs, greens, and microgreens for chefs. Its work emphasizes flavor, crop quality, soil health, sustainable agricultural practices, and collaboration between farmers and culinary professionals.
entities.roleUse:
A specific farm to consider when researching possible local farm partnerships for my community food-system and grocery-store ideas.

Because I met Farmer Lee Jones while attending culinary school, The Chef’s Garden is not an abstract example to me. It is a real Ohio farm whose agricultural and culinary work I have encountered and may want to study further or approach later.

Possible areas to explore include:

local crop sourcing
specialty and culturally useful crops
imperfect or surplus produce
chef-farmer collaboration
community food access
culinary education
soil-centered agriculture

This record does not state that The Chef’s Garden has agreed to participate in the project.

entities.name: Doctor Henry Feldman
entities.description:
Doctor Henry Feldman is a geneticist, biotechnology researcher, and manipulator whose pursuit of control begins with early experiments in subliminal influence. Raised with wealth but lacking genuine attention and guidance, he develops an obsession with power and control. After medical school, an organization recruits him because of his ability to influence and manipulate others.

Feldman publicly presents himself as a renowned scientist while secretly conducting experiments beyond ethical and legal limits. His work includes genetic manipulation, behavioral control, programmed compliance, and the use of ancient technology.
entities.roleUse:
Feldman is a central antagonist whose actions connect Kido’s testing, manipulation, reprogramming, the ancient device, The Order, the Russian Federation, Colonel Reed Hawkes, and the effort to turn Kido into a controllable instrument.

His need for control places him in direct opposition to Kido. Feldman’s role must be tracked carefully because his influence extends across several chapters, organizations, experiments, and covert relationships.

entities.name: The Order
entities.description:
The Order is a covert organization that operates as an unseen force shaping nations, economies, political power, scientific research, and human development. It provides protection and resources to Doctor Henry Feldman in exchange for research and results that serve the private goals of its members.

The organization is not united by one moral purpose. Its members support Feldman for different reasons, including profit, political dominance, enhanced soldiers, technological advancement, control, and the reshaping of humanity.
entities.roleUse:
The Order supports and protects Feldman’s illegal genetic, behavioral, and technological experiments. It gives him access to funding, test subjects, political influence, materials, and secrecy.

Its members include people from corporate, political, military, mercenary, and technological backgrounds. Their alliance is transactional, and each member expects Feldman’s work to advance a separate agenda.

The Order connects Feldman’s private experiments to broader political and institutional power.

entities.name: Kido Thompson
entities.description:
Kido Thompson is a Bajan man in his thirties. He is Black, with black hair and brown eyes. He is loving, kind, loyal, shy, and a good listener, but he struggles with anger when he believes he or someone else is being treated unjustly.

Kido’s interests include photography, computers, poetry, music, fencing, soccer, chess, and reading. His childhood and adolescence were shaped by family mistreatment, bullying, sexual abuse, placement in St. John’s Home for Boys, and leaving home during high school. Music teacher George Hinkson became the supportive father figure Kido had lacked.

Despite his trauma, Kido remains caring and empathetic. His past affects his ability to trust, his response to injustice, and his struggle to control the power that awakens after the Mirrian attack.
entities.roleUse:
Kido is the central character of Emperor’s Earth. After surviving the Mirrian attack, he develops extraordinary abilities and becomes a leader among the remaining survivors.

His power places him between two possible paths: becoming a protector and builder of a better future or becoming SHIVA, the destroyer of worlds. His story follows his struggle with trauma, anger, leadership, manipulation, responsibility, forgiveness, and the ethical use of power.

Kido becomes the focus of Doctor Feldman’s experiments and behavioral programming, the Russian Federation’s strategic interest, Colonel Reed Hawkes’s capture attempts, and the political concerns of the Mirrians. His relationships with Ricky Chapman, Ken Nakamura, Mira Devereaux, Xavier, and Ja-Jorel help anchor him when his identity and control are threatened.

entities.name: Colonel Reed Hawkes
entities.description:
Colonel Reed Hawkes is a former member of the United Terran Navy SEAL Division who later operates independently as a mercenary and security contractor.

His experience includes high-risk retrieval, perimeter operations, secure transportation, containment, and off-the-books assignments. He is discreet, tactically precise, emotionally controlled, and willing to work under different aliases. His loyalties are conditional and primarily tied to payment rather than politics or long-term allegiance.

Reed previously crossed paths with Mira Devereaux during her work as a war correspondent. Her records describe him as a one-time contact who guided her through a siege perimeter before becoming difficult to trace. Doctor Feldman later finds Reed through Mira’s archived reports and hires him to capture Kido.
entities.roleUse:
Reed enters the story when Doctor Feldman needs someone capable of locating, containing, and capturing Kido after Feldman’s programming begins to fail.

Feldman provides Reed with containment technology, including a neural dampener, and uses him in multiple attempts to trap Kido. Reed’s operations connect him to Warehouse 9B, Prospect Park, Coney Island, the safehouse, transit-disruption technology, and Feldman’s wider effort to regain control.

Reed initially treats Kido as a high-value target and a paid assignment. His later confrontation and confession reveal information about Feldman’s involvement and Reed’s own role in the capture attempts.

entities.name: Petrichor
entities.description: The distinctive earthy smell associated with rain falling on dry soil, clay, rock, pavement, or other porous surfaces, particularly after warm or dry weather.
entities.roleUse: Central subject of the poem and primary concept of the Zettel. Connects the creative note to definitions, scientific studies, sensory vocabulary, and future poems about rain.

entities.name: Geosmin
entities.description: An organic compound with an intense earthy or musty odor. Geosmin is associated with soil microorganisms and contributes to the smell of wet earth.
entities.roleUse: Supplies scientific context for the earthy component of petrichor. It should remain distinct from petrichor, which describes the broader sensory phenomenon.

entities.name: Rain Aerosol
entities.description: Microscopic airborne droplets or particles generated when raindrops strike porous surfaces such as soil. These aerosols can carry material and odors from the ground into the surrounding air.
entities.roleUse: xplains how the scent connected with petrichor travels from the ground into the air and reaches the speaker.

entities.name: I. J. Bear
entities.description: Australian researcher from the CSIRO Division of Mineral Chemistry who co-authored the 1964 paper “Nature of Argillaceous Odour.”
entities.roleUse: Historical researcher associated with the scientific investigation and naming of petrichor.

entities.name: R. G. Thomas
entities.description: ustralian researcher from the CSIRO Division of Mineral Chemistry who co-authored the 1964 paper “Nature of Argillaceous Odour.”
entities.roleUse: Historical researcher associated with the scientific investigation and naming of petrichor.

entities.name: Soil
entities.description: he upper layer of earth containing minerals, organic matter, water, air, and microorganisms. Dry soil can hold plant-derived substances and microbial compounds that become airborne when rain strikes it.
entities.roleUse: Primary physical surface in the poem. Provides the ground, texture, dryness, color change, and earthy scent associated with the arrival of rain.

entities.name: Raindrop
entities.description: A drop of atmospheric water that falls to the ground. Its impact on porous soil can trap and release tiny air bubbles and aerosols.
entities.roleUse: Provides the poem’s first visible and physical action. The raindrop connects the dry surface to the release of scent.

entities.name: Clay
entities.description: A fine-grained natural material that can retain substances associated with the characteristic odor released after dry conditions and rainfall.
entities.roleUse: Provides historical and material context for the phrase “argillaceous odour.” It can also supply grounded images of mineral earth becoming wet.

entities.name: Handedness
entities.description: Natural hand dominance, discussed as part of neurological organization rather than simply a behavioral preference.
entities.roleUse: Central concept connecting left-handedness, motor function, forced switching, development, and expression.

entities.name: Forced Hand Switching
entities.description: The practice of preventing a person, especially a child, from using their naturally dominant hand and requiring use of the opposite hand.
entities.roleUse: Central experience being examined for its possible physical, psychological, developmental, and expressive effects.

entities.name: Left-Handedness Stigma
entities.description: Cultural or social beliefs that portray left-handedness as wrong, undesirable, dangerous, or associated with evil.
entities.roleUse: Provides cultural context for punishment, correction, shame, labeling, and suppression of natural handedness.

entities.name: Adaptive Expression
entities.description: The idea that suppression or redirection of natural behavior may lead a person to develop alternative ways of observing, processing, and expressing experience.
entities.roleUse: Connects childhood adaptation with later sensory, emotional, observational, and creative expression.

entities.name: Sensory Processing
entities.description: Processing experience through visual, spatial, physical, auditory, emotional, and environmental information.
entities.roleUse: Used in the document to explain the proposed relationship between neurological adaptation and sensory-centered expression.

entities.name: André Darlington
entities.description: Author and drinks writer. Co-author of The New Cocktail Hour: The Essential Guide to Handcrafted Drinks.
entities.roleUse: Author; source creator

entities.name: Tenaya Darlington
entities.description: Author and food and drinks writer. Co-author of The New Cocktail Hour: The Essential Guide to Handcrafted Drinks.
entities.roleUse: Author; source creator

entities.name: Marie-Antoine Carême
entities.description: French chef and culinary authority who helped systematize and codify classical French cuisine. Carême is associated with the development of grande cuisine and with organizing culinary preparations, including sauces, into defined systems that influenced later professional cooking.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development and codification of classical French cuisine.

entities.name: Georges-Auguste Escoffier
entities.description: French chef who modernized and systematized professional cookery, building on the foundations of classical French cuisine. Escoffier simplified and reorganized earlier culinary practices and is particularly associated with the organization of the professional kitchen and the modernization of classical cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; modernization and organization of professional cookery and classical French cuisine.

entities.name: Cultural Stigma
entities.description: Description: Negative cultural meanings, judgments, beliefs, or social expectations attached to a trait, behavior, identity, or difference. Cultural stigma may continue to influence self-perception, social behavior, relationships, and feelings of belonging even after the original practice or pressure that reinforced it has ended.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine how socially learned judgments can remain psychologically or socially significant after direct correction, punishment, or suppression stops.

entities.name: Guillaume Tirel
entities.description: Medieval French cook, usually known as Taillevent, born around 1310. He is associated with Le Viandier and with refining earlier cooking practices by reducing reliance on heavy spices and emphasizing the natural flavors of foods.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of sauces, soups, and refined medieval French cooking.

entities.name: Le Viandier
entities.description: Important late-medieval cookbook associated with Guillaume Tirel, known as Taillevent. Written before the invention of the printing press, handwritten copies remained in use for more than a century. It was printed in 1490 and is described in the source as possibly the first cookbook ever printed.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary text; reference for medieval French cooking, sauces, soups, and the development of written culinary practice.

entities.name: François-Pierre de La Varenne
entities.description: French cook and author, 1615–1678, associated with Le Cuisinier François. His work helped present recipes and cooking techniques in a more orderly and systematic form than earlier unsystematic collections.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; organization and systematization of seventeenth-century French cooking practices.

entities.name: Le Cuisinier François
entities.description: Cookbook by François-Pierre de La Varenne, published in 1651. It summarized cooking practices used in aristocratic households and was among the early works to organize recipes and cooking techniques systematically. It remained an important reference for cooks for more than 150 years.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary text; reference for seventeenth-century French cooking and the development of systematic recipe and technique presentation.

entities.name: Slow Food
entities.description: International food movement concerned with preserving local food traditions, encouraging greater awareness of where food comes from and how it tastes, and supporting sustainable and ecologically responsible agriculture. Over time, the movement expanded its focus to include issues such as race, poverty, hunger, environmental concerns, climate change, and stewardship of the land.
entities.roleUse: Used to study food culture, sustainability, local food traditions, agricultural practices, food awareness, environmental responsibility, and social issues connected to food systems.

entities.name: Fernand Point
entities.description: French chef, 1897–1955, who simplified and lightened classical cuisine at his restaurant La Pyramide in Vienne, France. Point emphasized perfection, careful development of dishes, and meals of exceptional quality. His approach strongly influenced the generation of chefs who later developed nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; transition from classical cuisine toward lighter twentieth-century French cooking and influence on nouvelle cuisine.

entities.name: La Pyramide
entities.description: Restaurant in Vienne, France, associated with chef Fernand Point. It became an important center of twentieth-century French cooking and the training ground for chefs who later became influential figures in nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; site of Fernand Point's culinary work and training of influential twentieth-century chefs.

entities.name: Paul Bocuse
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who became one of the prominent chefs associated with nouvelle cuisine during the twentieth century.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development and promotion of nouvelle cuisine.

entities.name: Jean Troisgros
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who became one of the influential chefs associated with nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of nouvelle cuisine and lighter approaches to classical French cooking.

entities.name: Pierre Troisgros
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who became one of the influential chefs associated with nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of nouvelle cuisine and lighter approaches to classical French cooking.

entities.name: Alain Chapel
entities.description: French chef and former apprentice of Fernand Point who later became an important figure in twentieth-century French cooking and nouvelle cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of nouvelle cuisine.

entities.name: Nouvelle Cuisine
entities.description: Twentieth-century French culinary movement associated with chefs who reacted against heavy and overly complicated classical cuisine. It emphasized simpler and more natural flavors, lighter sauces and seasonings, shorter cooking times, reduced reliance on flour-thickened sauces, and artistic plating performed by the chef in the kitchen. Although the movement later became associated with excessive and elaborate presentations, many of its strongest ideas became incorporated into modern classical cooking.
entities.roleUse: Used to study the evolution of modern French cuisine, reactions to classical cuisine, lighter cooking methods, natural flavors, and chef-driven plating.

entities.name: Alice Waters
entities.description: American restaurateur and chef associated with the opening of Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, in 1971. Her culinary philosophy emphasizes that good food depends on high-quality ingredients and favors seasonal, locally grown, organically raised products prepared simply.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of ingredient-focused, seasonal, local, and sustainable approaches to modern North American cooking.

entities.name: Chez Panisse
entities.description: Restaurant opened by Alice Waters in Berkeley, California, in 1971. Its emphasis on high-quality seasonal and locally produced ingredients became influential in the development of modern North American cooking and the broader local-food movement.
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; example of ingredient-focused, seasonal, local, and sustainable restaurant cooking.

entities.name: Larry Forgione
entities.description: American chef who promoted local ingredients and regional American cuisine through his New York City restaurant An American Place, following the growing emphasis on ingredient quality established by chefs such as Alice Waters.
entities.roleUse: Historical culinary figure; development of local and regional ingredient-focused American cuisine.

entities.name: An American Place
entities.description: New York City restaurant associated with chef Larry Forgione and the promotion of local ingredients and regional American cuisine.
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; example of the growth of local-ingredient and regional American cooking.

entities.name: Sustainable Agriculture
entities.description: Agricultural approach intended to produce healthful food while supporting economically viable farms and farming communities, providing fair working conditions, preserving soil, water, and air, treating animals humanely, and maintaining farmland productivity over the long term.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine the relationship between food production, environmental stewardship, farm economics, labor practices, animal welfare, and culinary sourcing.

entities.name: Organic Food
entities.description: Food produced according to standards that restrict or exclude specified artificial chemicals, drugs, and other prohibited agricultural inputs, allowing qualifying products to carry an organic designation.
entities.roleUse: Used to study agricultural production methods, ingredient sourcing, food labeling, sustainability, and consumer food choices.

entities.name: Biodynamic Agriculture
entities.description: Agricultural system that emphasizes natural soil nutrients such as compost and manure, avoids pesticides, herbicides, and other artificial chemicals, and treats soil, crops, and animals as parts of a single interconnected system. Biodynamic agriculture also incorporates cosmic forces and spiritual concepts into planting and harvesting practices.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine holistic agricultural systems, sustainability, soil management, natural agricultural inputs, farming philosophy, and alternatives to conventional agriculture.

entities.name: Heirloom Varieties
entities.description: Older varieties of fruits and vegetables that existed before industrial agriculture increasingly favored hybrids bred for higher productivity, mechanized harvesting, durability, and long-distance shipping. Heirloom varieties are often valued for flavor, texture, genetic diversity, and their connection to agricultural traditions.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine ingredient quality, agricultural biodiversity, flavor, sustainability, and the effects of industrial agriculture on food varieties.

entities.name: Farm-to-Table
entities.description: Food movement emphasizing the use of locally produced foods sourced from nearby farms, fisheries, ranches, and other producers. Farm-to-table restaurants often identify producers, emphasize ingredient provenance, and develop closer relationships between chefs, consumers, and local food producers.
entities.roleUse: Used to study local sourcing, ingredient provenance, restaurant purchasing, food-system transparency, freshness, sustainability, and relationships between chefs and producers.

entities.name: Indigenous Cuisine
entities.description: Cuisine based on foods and foodways of Indigenous peoples that existed within a region before European colonization. In the North American context described by the source, it emphasizes native wild and cultivated foods while excluding crops and livestock introduced by later European and other settlers.
entities.roleUse: Used to study Indigenous foodways, regional food systems, native ingredients, precolonial cuisine, cultural food history, and relationships between cuisine and place.

entities.name: Genetically Modified Organisms
entities.description: Plants or animals whose genes have been artificially altered to produce desired characteristics, such as increased productivity, disease resistance, or herbicide resistance. Their use is debated in relation to crop yields, land use, food safety, long-term health effects, and agricultural sustainability.
entities.roleUse: Used to examine genetic modification in agriculture, food production, food safety, sustainability, crop productivity, and debates surrounding modern agricultural technology.

entities.description: Agricultural approach that emphasizes natural soil nutrients, including compost and manure, while restricting or avoiding pesticides, herbicides, and other artificial chemicals. In the source, organic agriculture serves as a point of comparison for biodynamic agriculture.
entities.name: Organic Agriculture
entities.roleUse: Used to examine agricultural production methods, natural soil management, chemical avoidance, sustainability, ingredient sourcing, and relationships between organic and biodynamic farming systems.

entities.description: Precision cooking technique that uses controlled temperatures and cooking times to produce consistent results and can create new textures and flavors in familiar foods.
entities.name: Sous Vide
entities.roleUse: Used to examine precision cooking, temperature control, modern culinary technology, texture development, and controlled food preparation.

entities.description: Computer-controlled process that builds three-dimensional objects by depositing material layer upon layer. In culinary applications, 3D printers may use food powders, pastes, or gels to create garnishes, components, or potentially entire meals.
entities.name: 3D Printing
entities.roleUse: Used to examine digital fabrication in food preparation, automated food production, culinary design, food presentation, and emerging kitchen technologies.

entities.description: Manufacturing process in which a three-dimensional object is constructed by adding successive layers of material according to instructions controlled by a computer program. 3D printing is a form of additive manufacturing.
entities.name: Additive Manufacturing
entities.roleUse: Used to examine the underlying production principle of 3D printing and its application to culinary technology and food fabrication.

entities.description: Spanish chef associated with El Bulli who pioneered experimental approaches to cooking involving gels, foams, powders, infusions, extracts, and other unconventional methods of presenting flavors, textures, and aromas.
entities.name: Ferran Adrià
entities.roleUse: Historical and contemporary culinary figure; experimentation with modern cooking techniques, food transformation, texture, flavor, aroma, and molecular gastronomy.

entities.description: Acclaimed Spanish restaurant associated with chef Ferran Adrià and known for pioneering experimental approaches to flavor, texture, aroma, presentation, and modern culinary techniques.
entities.name: El Bulli
entities.roleUse: Historical restaurant; site of experimentation and development associated with molecular gastronomy and modernist culinary techniques.

entities.description: Approach to food and cooking that explores how scientific principles and modern techniques can produce new forms of flavor, texture, aroma, and presentation. Techniques may involve gels, foams, powders, infusions, extracts, natural gums, gelatin, pectin, and other ingredients used in unconventional ways.
entities.name: Molecular Gastronomy
entities.roleUse: Used to examine relationships between science, technology, ingredients, culinary technique, sensory experience, and innovative food presentation.

entities.description: French chemist associated with research into the scientific principles of cooking and credited in the source with coining the term molecular gastronomy.
entities.name: Hervé This
entities.roleUse: Scientific and culinary research figure; development and study of molecular gastronomy and the application of chemistry to food and cooking.

entities.description: Modern approach to cooking associated with the application of science, technology, unconventional ingredients, and experimental techniques to transform flavors, textures, aromas, and food presentation. The term was popularized by Nathan Myhrvold through his books of the same name.
entities.name: Modernist Cuisine
entities.roleUse: Used to examine technologically and scientifically informed culinary experimentation and the adaptation of modern techniques into professional cooking.

entities.description: Author and food researcher associated with popularizing the term modernist cuisine through the multivolume book collection Modernist Cuisine.
entities.name: Nathan Myhrvold
entities.roleUse: Culinary research and publishing figure; popularization and documentation of modernist cuisine and science-based cooking.

aliases: Modernist Cuisine: The Art and Science of Cooking
entities.description: Multivolume culinary work associated with Nathan Myhrvold that helped popularize the term modernist cuisine and documents scientific, technological, and experimental approaches to food and cooking.
entities.name: Modernist Cuisine
entities.roleUse: Culinary reference work; source for modernist cooking techniques, food science, culinary technology, and experimental food preparation.

entities.description: English chef associated with the use and development of molecular gastronomy and modernist culinary techniques.
entities.name: Heston Blumenthal
entities.roleUse: Culinary figure; experimentation with science, technology, flavor, texture, and modernist cooking techniques.

entities.description: North American chef associated with experimentation in molecular gastronomy and modernist cuisine.

entities.description: North American chef associated with molecular gastronomy, modernist cuisine, and experimentation with science, technology, flavor, texture, and food presentation.

entities.name: Homaro Cantu

entities.description: Any substance in food capable of causing illness or injury. Food hazards are categorized as biological hazards, chemical hazards, physical hazards, and allergens.
entities.roleUse: Foundational food-safety concept used to classify and analyze risks associated with ingredients, handling, preparation, storage, and service.

entities.name: Pathogen
entities.description: A microorganism capable of causing disease. Foodborne pathogens may include bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites.
entities.roleUse: Used in food-safety, microbiology, sanitation, HACCP, and foodborne-illness research.

entities.name: Water Activity
entities.description: Measurement of the water available for microbial use in food, expressed as aw on a scale from 0 to 1.0. Water activity influences whether microorganisms can grow in a food
entities.roleUse: Used when analyzing microbial growth, preservation, fermentation, curing, dehydration, salt concentration, sugar concentration, and shelf stability.

entities.name: pH
entities.description: Measurement of acidity or alkalinity on a scale from 0 to 14, with 7 representing neutrality. pH affects the ability of foodborne pathogens to grow.
entities.roleUse: Used in food-safety analysis, fermentation, acidification, pickling, preservation, recipe development, and microbial-growth control.

entities.name: TCS Food
entities.description: Food requiring time and temperature control for safety because its characteristics can provide conditions favorable to the growth of disease-causing microorganisms.
entities.roleUse: Used to classify ingredients and prepared foods requiring controlled handling, storage, preparation, holding, transportation, and service.

entities.name: Food Danger Zone
entities.description: Temperature range identified in the chapter as 40°F–140°F (4°C–60°C), within which disease-causing bacteria can grow rapidly.
entities.roleUse: Used when developing procedures for food storage, preparation, cooling, reheating, transportation, and hot or cold holding.

entities.name: Cross-Contamination
entities.description: Transfer of harmful microorganisms or contaminants between foods, people, equipment, utensils, surfaces, water, pests, or other carriers. The chapter establishes that bacteria must be carried from one location to another rather than moving independently.
entities.roleUse: Used in kitchen workflow design, sanitation procedures, food handling, equipment separation, allergen management, and HACCP planning.

entities.name: Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point
entities.description: A systematic food-safety program that identifies possible danger points in food operations and establishes procedures for corrective action.
entities.roleUse: Framework for systematically identifying, controlling, monitoring, and correcting food-safety hazards in food-service operations.
aliases: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point

entities.name: Sanitizing
entities.description: Process of killing disease-causing bacteria on dishes, equipment, and other appropriate surfaces through sufficient heat or approved chemical methods.
entities.roleUse: Used in warewashing, equipment sanitation, food-contact surface procedures, kitchen SOPs, and food-safety training.

entities.name: Foodborne Illness
entities.description: Illness resulting from foodborne hazards, particularly contaminated food containing pathogenic microorganisms or their toxins.
entities.roleUse: Umbrella entity for connecting food hazards, pathogens, diseases, contamination pathways, preventive controls, sanitation procedures, and HACCP notes.

entities.name: Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point
entities.description: A systematic food-safety program used by food-service establishments to identify potential food-safety danger points and establish procedures for corrective action. The chapter presents HACCP as a practical system for putting food-safety principles into systematic operation.
entities.roleUse: Used as the overall food-safety management system for identifying hazards, determining where controls are necessary, monitoring food-safety processes, and establishing corrective actions within food-service operations.
aliases: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point
Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point System

entities.name: Critical Control Point
entities.description: A point, step, or procedure within a HACCP system where control is applied to address a significant food-safety hazard. A CCP represents a specific control location within the larger HACCP process rather than the food-safety system itself.
entities.roleUse: Used within HACCP planning to identify specific stages of food handling or production where control is necessary to prevent, eliminate, or reduce a food-safety hazard to an acceptable level.

entities.name: Standard Operating Procedure
entities.description: A documented set of standardized instructions that establishes how a specific task or operational process should be performed consistently. In food-service operations, SOPs can formalize procedures for sanitation, food handling, storage, cleaning, employee hygiene, temperature control, pest control, and workplace safety
entities.roleUse: Used to document repeatable operational procedures, establish consistent work practices, support employee training, define food-safety responsibilities, and provide procedures that support HACCP and other food-safety controls.

entities.name: I Built the Dungeon That Killed Me
entities.description: A poetry concept centered on a speaker who gradually constructs the very dungeon that ultimately confines or destroys them. The construction occurs over time through accumulated choices, habits, actions, or repeated acts whose consequences may not be understood while they are happening. The dungeon should remain concrete in the poem: doors, locks, walls, keys, mortar, rooms, foundations, and individual stones. Its meaning should emerge through the progression of the poem rather than being defined in advance. The central unresolved question is: If I built it, why can't I leave it? Possible thematic meanings include self-sabotage, grief, addiction, ambition, isolation, guilt, identity,
entities.roleUse: Use as the central conceptual entity for developing a poem based on self-created confinement and its consequences. The poem may move through: foundation → construction → recognition → entrapment → consequence Preserve the sense of gradual accumulation: stone follows stone, choice follows choice. Allow emotion to emerge through that accumulation rather than through direct explanation. Do not determine what the dungeon ultimately represents before drafting. Its meaning should be discovered through the poem itself, and the central question may remain unanswered.

entities.name: Ricky Chapman
entities.description:
Age: 32

Ethnicity: Black

Gender: Male

Appearance: He has black hair, brown eyes, and a muscular build. He has tattoos on his arms and chest, and often wears casual clothes, such as T-shirts and jeans.

Personality: Impulsive, rebellious, hot-headed, loyal to those he cares about, and struggles with addiction and substance abuse.

Background: Grew up in a rough neighborhood and had a troubled childhood, often getting into fights and trouble with the law. Despite his tough exterior, he has a soft spot for those he cares about and is fiercely loyal to his friends. He fell into a life of drug use and crime, which caused him to be in and out of prison. His girlfriend cheated on him with his best friend while he was in prison, leading him to choose Kido as his new partner and support system.

Interests/Hobbies: He enjoys drawing and sketching, has a talent for graffiti art, listens to music, and plays video games.

Goals/Motivations: To turn his life around, stay out of trouble, support his children, make amends for past mistakes, help Kido, and be a good partner to him.

Challenges/Obstacles: Struggling with addiction and avoiding trouble with the law, while dealing with his past mistakes and their consequences.

Relationship with Other Characters: He is Kido’s partner, cares deeply for him, and wants to support him in any way he can. He has a tense relationship with Doctor Feldman, whom he distrusts and believes is manipulating Kido.
entities.roleUse: Character in the story. Kido’s partner and support system.

entities.name: Kenji "Ken" Nakamura
entities.description:
Age: 35

Ethnicity: Japanese-American

Gender: Male

Appearance: Short black hair, dark brown eyes, glasses, average build.

Personality: Intelligent, analytical, introverted, perfectionist, tends to overthink things.

Hobbies/Interests: Science, technology, video games, hiking.

Background: Ken grew up in a traditional Japanese family that placed a strong emphasis on academic achievement. He excelled in school and earned a PhD in molecular biology. He's worked in the lab with Kido for several years and admires Kido's creativity and passion for science. Despite being introverted, Ken has developed a close bond with Kido and considers him a trusted friend. However, he sometimes struggles with anxiety and can be overly cautious in his work.
entities.roleUse: Character in the story. Kido’s laboratory colleague and trusted friend.

entities.name: Mira Devereaux
entities.description:
Age: 36

Occupation: Journalist

Ethnicity: French

Gender: Female

Appearance: Mira has long, black, wavy hair and green eyes. She is 5'8" with an athletic build.

Background: Mira was born and raised in France to a family of journalists. She inherited her passion for uncovering the truth from her parents and followed in their footsteps. Mira moved to the United States to work for a prominent news outlet before the Mirrain attack. She lost everything in the following chaos and was forced to adapt to survive. She received military training to protect herself and those she cared about. Despite her training, Mira retains her journalistic curiosity and often puts herself in dangerous situations to uncover the truth.

Personality: Mira is determined, strong-willed, and fiercely loyal to her friends. She values the truth above all else and isn't afraid to put herself in danger to uncover it. Her military training has made her quick-thinking and resourceful, but she still struggles with the trauma of the Mirrain attack.
entities.roleUse: Character in the story. Journalist whose pursuit of the truth continues after the Mirrain attack.

entities.name: Tiny Garden Habit
entities.description: Gardening content publisher that creates educational gardening information, infographics, and social-media content. Tiny Garden Habit published the Facebook infographic “Brush These 5 Herbs for a Burst of Fragrance” and the accompanying observations about aromatic herbs, plant placement, containment, growing conditions, and basil harvesting.
entities.roleUse: Source creator and publisher for gardening and culinary-gardening reference material.

entities.name: Mint
entities.description: An aromatic culinary herb known for its fresh, cool fragrance. Lightly rubbing, pinching, or brushing the leaves makes its aroma more noticeable. Mint spreads readily through underground runners and can become aggressive when planted directly in an unrestricted garden bed.
entities.roleUse: Culinary herb used for cooking, beverages, garnishes, aromatic gardening, sensory study, and garden-to-kitchen ingredient research.

entities.name: Lemon Balm
entities.description: An aromatic herb known for its bright lemon-like fragrance. Rubbing or lightly crushing the leaves makes the citrus-like aroma more noticeable. Lemon balm can spread aggressively and may be better contained when grown in a managed culinary garden.
entities.roleUse: Aromatic and culinary herb used for beverages, culinary applications, sensory study, herb gardening, and garden-to-kitchen ingredient research.

entities.name: Rosemary
entities.description: A woody aromatic culinary herb known for its strong piney and resinous fragrance. Brushing or rubbing the foliage makes its aroma more noticeable. Rosemary grows best in sunny locations with well-drained soil and can be positioned near paths where incidental contact releases fragrance.
entities.roleUse: Culinary herb used in savory cooking, aromatic gardening, sensory study, herb cultivation, and garden-to-kitchen ingredient research.

entities.name: Thyme
entities.description: A compact aromatic culinary herb known for its warm, herbal fragrance. Light rubbing or brushing of the leaves makes its aroma more noticeable. Thyme favors sunny conditions and well-drained soil and can be grown near paths or borders where movement may release its fragrance.
entities.roleUse: Culinary herb used in savory cooking, herb gardening, sensory study, aromatic garden design, and garden-to-kitchen ingredient research.

entities.name: Basil
entities.description: A tender aromatic culinary herb known for sweet and spicy aromatic characteristics. Lightly rubbing or handling the leaves makes its fragrance more noticeable. Regular harvesting of the growing tips during warm weather encourages continued production of fresh leafy growth.
entities.roleUse: Culinary herb used in cooking, sauces, garnishes, herb gardening, sensory study, harvesting research, and garden-to-kitchen ingredient development.
