revisions.title: Kireji Creates a Cut Between Parts of a Haiku
revisions.content: Kireji is a Japanese cutting word that creates emphasis, pause, emotional resonance, or a shift between parts of a haiku while allowing meaning to arise from the relationship between them.

snapshot.title: Kireji Creates a Cut Between Parts of a Haiku
snapshot.mainIdea: Kireji is a Japanese cutting word that creates emphasis, pause, emotional resonance, or a shift between parts of a haiku while allowing meaning to arise from the relationship between them.
snapshot.body:
Kireji helps keep two images or perceptions separate without completely disconnecting them.

The cut creates space between the parts of the poem. That space can produce contrast, tension, emphasis, reflection, or an emotional shift.

The cut may occur after the first five morae or after the following seven morae. Its position helps determine whether the poem moves as 5/7-5 or 5-7/5.

English punctuation can approximate some effects of kireji, but it is not an exact equivalent. A dash, colon, semicolon, ellipsis, or line break may suggest a pause or division, but Japanese cutting words also carry grammatical, tonal, and emotional functions.

Common kireji should therefore be studied within Japanese language and poetic context rather than treated as interchangeable forms of punctuation.

revisions.title: Haiku Developed from the Opening Verse of Linked Poetry
revisions.content: Haiku developed from hokku, the opening verse of Japanese linked poetry, where season, atmosphere, placement, and the relationship among images were established at the beginning of the sequence.

snapshot.title: Haiku Developed from the Opening Verse of Linked Poetry
snapshot.mainIdea: Haiku developed from hokku, the opening verse of Japanese linked poetry, where season, atmosphere, placement, and the relationship among images were established at the beginning of the sequence.
snapshot.body:
Haiku should not be understood only as an isolated three-line form.

Its history is connected to hokku, the opening verse of Japanese linked poetry. The hokku established the season, atmosphere, and an initial relationship among images for the verses that followed.

Understanding this origin helps explain why season, brevity, placement, and the cut remain important within haiku.

The form later developed into an independent poem, but some of its central features still reflect the function of the earlier opening verse.

Studying linked-verse traditions provides a stronger historical foundation than beginning with later English classroom definitions of haiku.

revisions.content: A haiku often contains two images, perceptions, or parts placed beside one another by a cut, allowing contrast, connection, tension, or recognition to develop without the poet explaining the conclusion.

snapshot.title: Haiku Often Moves Through Two Parts Rather Than Three Statements
snapshot.mainIdea: A haiku often contains two images, perceptions, or parts placed beside one another by a cut, allowing contrast, connection, tension, or recognition to develop without the poet explaining the conclusion.
snapshot.body:
Body
The three sections of a haiku should not automatically be treated as three independent statements.

A haiku often moves through two parts:

First image / second image

The movement may also appear as a fragment and a phrase.

The cut keeps the two parts distinct while placing them in relationship. Meaning develops through what happens between them rather than through a direct explanation from the poet.

The reader experiences the contrast, connection, tension, or recognition and participates in forming the meaning.

This structure should not be treated as an introduction, explanation, and conclusion.

revisions.title: How sustainable is artificial intelligence?
revisions.content: Artificial intelligence may offer useful tools and solutions, but I need to examine whether the energy, water, hardware, infrastructure, and other resources required to build and operate AI make its continued expansion environmentally sustainable.

snapshot.title: How sustainable is artificial intelligence?
snapshot.mainIdea: Artificial intelligence may offer useful tools and solutions, but I need to examine whether the energy, water, hardware, infrastructure, and other resources required to build and operate AI make its continued expansion environmentally sustainable.
snapshot.body:
My concern is how sustainable artificial intelligence actually is, beginning with what is required to power it.

AI systems depend on data centers, electricity, computer hardware, cooling systems, network infrastructure, storage, maintenance, and continued equipment replacement. I want to understand the environmental effects associated with training AI models, operating them, storing information, and processing individual requests.

The concern is not limited to electricity. I also need to consider the water used for cooling, the materials and minerals required to manufacture computer hardware, the environmental effects of producing and transporting that equipment, and what happens when the hardware is replaced or discarded.

I want to understand where the energy used by AI infrastructure comes from and whether claims about renewable energy reflect the complete environmental cost. A company may power part of its operation with renewable electricity while still depending on resource extraction, manufacturing, water use, construction, transportation, and electronic waste.

AI may also be used to support sustainability through research, energy management, agriculture, climate modeling, waste reduction, transportation, and other applications. However, those possible benefits do not automatically make AI itself sustainable.

The question is whether the environmental benefits created through AI can justify or outweigh the resources consumed by the systems supporting it.

I also want to examine who receives the benefits of AI and who bears the environmental costs of its infrastructure. Data centers, energy production, water use, mineral extraction, manufacturing, and electronic waste may affect communities that do not receive equal benefits from the technology.

This note is not based on a conclusion that AI is sustainable or unsustainable. It establishes the questions I need to investigate before reaching a conclusion.

subtype.name: Question
subtype.description: Processed question, inquiry, or issue needing further study.

originFleetingNoteId.rawCapture:
How sustainable is artificial intelligence?

AI requires energy to power data centers, train models, process requests, store information, and operate the infrastructure supporting it. I want to understand where that energy comes from, how much is required, and what environmental effects result from the growing use of AI.

The concern is not limited to electricity. AI may also require water for cooling data centers, physical land and buildings, computer hardware, minerals, manufacturing, transportation, maintenance, and the replacement or disposal of equipment.

I want to examine whether the benefits and uses of AI justify the resources it consumes, how its environmental impact is measured, and whether companies are accurately reporting that impact.

I also want to study whether AI can contribute to sustainability while simultaneously creating its own sustainability problems. The question is not simply whether AI is useful, but whether the systems supporting it can continue expanding without causing unacceptable environmental and resource costs.

revisions.title: English Haiku Preserves the 5-7-5 Numbers but Changes the Sound Measure
revisions.content: English-language haiku often translate the Japanese 5-7-5 mora pattern into five, seven, and five syllables, preserving the numbers while changing the original sound measurement.

snapshot.title: English Haiku Preserves the 5-7-5 Numbers but Changes the Sound Measure
snapshot.mainIdea: English-language haiku often translate the Japanese 5-7-5 mora pattern into five, seven, and five syllables, preserving the numbers while changing the original sound measurement.
snapshot.body:
The traditional Japanese 5-7-5 pattern counts morae rather than English syllables.

When the pattern is adapted into English as five-, seven-, and five-syllable forms, the numerical arrangement remains, but the sound structure changes.

English syllables often carry more language than Japanese morae. Because of this, a seventeen-syllable English haiku can feel heavier, fuller, or more crowded than a seventeen-mora Japanese haiku.

Japanese haiku should therefore be studied before treating the English adaptation as equivalent to the original form.

In English-language haiku, meaning, season, cut, observation, and restraint may be more important than reproducing seventeen English syllables.

Writing simple haiku in Japanese may also help make the original rhythm and sound measurement easier to understand.

revisions.title: Growing Crops in Food Deserts
revisions.content: Community growing spaces could increase access to fresh food in food deserts by producing crops within or near the communities that need them.

snapshot.title: Growing Crops in Food Deserts
snapshot.mainIdea: Community growing spaces could increase access to fresh food in food deserts by producing crops within or near the communities that need them.
snapshot.body:
Growing crops in food deserts could connect sustainability, food access, community participation, and culinary knowledge.

Community gardens, rooftop gardens, indoor growing systems, vacant lots, and other available spaces could be used to produce food closer to where people live. The purpose would not only be to create green spaces but to increase access to fresh ingredients in communities where that access is limited.

The crops grown should be connected to what the community actually eats. Culinary knowledge can help determine which vegetables, herbs, fruits, and other crops would be useful, culturally relevant, adaptable to local growing conditions, and capable of supporting affordable meals.

The system could also include education about preparing, preserving, and using the harvest. Surplus crops could be distributed, sold affordably, preserved, or connected to a community grocery store.

This idea connects food production with what happens after harvest. Growing food alone does not guarantee access. Distribution, affordability, culinary knowledge, storage, preservation, and community participation must also be considered.

Potential Agricultural Connection

One place I already have in mind is The Chef’s Garden in Huron, Ohio. I met Farmer Lee Jones while I was attending culinary school.

His work and the farm’s connection between agriculture, chefs, specialty crops, sustainability, and culinary education make them relevant to this idea. I may want to study their model further or eventually explore whether they could offer knowledge, guidance, sourcing, collaboration, or another form of connection.

At this stage, this is a possible direction to investigate, not an established partnership.

revisions.content: Acid cuts through richness by adding brightness and contrast, making heavy foods feel cleaner and more complete on the palate.

snapshot.title: Acid Balances Richness Through Brightness and Contrast
snapshot.mainIdea: Acid cuts through richness by adding brightness and contrast, making heavy foods feel cleaner and more complete on the palate.
snapshot.body:
Rich foods can become heavy or tiring when fat, dairy, sweetness, or dense textures dominate the palate.
Acid creates contrast. It sharpens flavor, reduces the sense of heaviness, and helps separate one bite from the next.
The purpose of acid is not simply to make a dish taste sour. Used correctly, it brings balance by lifting other flavors and making the dish feel more complete.
This principle can be applied through ingredients such as citrus, vinegar, fermented products, wine, tomatoes, or cultured dairy, depending on the dish.

revisions.title: Cumulative Alcohol and Palate Perception Are Not the Same as Individual Beverage ABV
revisions.content: Cumulative alcohol across a tasting menu should be studied separately from the sensory effects of alcohol concentration within one beverage. Existing research establishes that ethanol changes taste, irritation, aroma, and mouthfeel and that tasting order can change perception, but this does not by itself prove exactly how progressive intoxication across a multi-course meal changes palate sensitivity.

snapshot.title: Cumulative Alcohol and Palate Perception Are Not the Same as Individual Beverage ABV
snapshot.mainIdea: Cumulative alcohol across a tasting menu should be studied separately from the sensory effects of alcohol concentration within one beverage. Existing research establishes that ethanol changes taste, irritation, aroma, and mouthfeel and that tasting order can change perception, but this does not by itself prove exactly how progressive intoxication across a multi-course meal changes palate sensitivity.
snapshot.body:
There are two related but different questions within tasting-menu beverage research.

The first concerns the local sensory effect of ethanol.

Each alcoholic beverage can affect bitterness, sweetness, oral irritation, aroma release, body, warmth, astringency, and other aspects of sensory perception. These effects occur because ethanol is physically present in the beverage.

The second concerns cumulative alcohol exposure across the meal.

As a guest consumes successive alcoholic pairings, total alcohol consumption increases. At the same time, the palate experiences repeated exposure to ethanol, food, acidity, sweetness, bitterness, spice, fat, tannin, carbonation, temperature, and other sensory stimuli.

Existing sensory research supports the idea that beverage order matters and that ethanol changes individual sensory experiences.

However, that evidence should not automatically be converted into the claim that cumulative alcohol simply “dulls the palate.”

A tasting menu introduces several possible causes of changes in later-course perception:

repeated ethanol exposure,

sensory adaptation,

oral irritation,

sensory fatigue,

food-related palate effects,

beverage ordering,

and increasing physiological intoxication.

These mechanisms need to be separated when researching cumulative alcohol.

This makes cumulative palate perception a broader research problem rather than a single established effect.

For tasting-menu development, the practical research question becomes:

How does the combined effect of repeated ethanol exposure, beverage ordering, sensory fatigue, food progression, and increasing alcohol consumption change the way later courses and pairings are perceived?

revisions.title: Ethanol Is a Sensory Component, Not Just an Intoxicant
revisions.content: Alcohol affects beverage perception before intoxication is considered because ethanol itself produces taste and chemesthetic sensations. It can contribute bitterness, sweetness, warmth, burning, and irritation, meaning changes in ABV can directly change how a beverage is experienced on the palate.

snapshot.title: Ethanol Is a Sensory Component, Not Just an Intoxicant
snapshot.mainIdea: Alcohol affects beverage perception before intoxication is considered because ethanol itself produces taste and chemesthetic sensations. It can contribute bitterness, sweetness, warmth, burning, and irritation, meaning changes in ABV can directly change how a beverage is experienced on the palate.
snapshot.body:
Ethanol should not be treated only as the substance responsible for intoxication. It is itself part of the sensory composition of an alcoholic beverage.

Human sensory research identifies ethanol as producing both taste and chemesthetic sensations. Bitterness and oral irritation are particularly important, while sweetness can also contribute depending on concentration and the beverage matrix.

The burning or warming sensation associated with alcohol is therefore different from ordinary taste. It contributes to the physical sensation of drinking and can increase the perceived intensity of a beverage.

Ethanol can also interact with other tastes rather than simply adding its own sensation. Acute ethanol exposure has been shown to suppress the immediate bitterness of quinine while increasing its bitter aftertaste, demonstrating that alcohol can modify how another taste stimulus is perceived.

Research using ethanol and sweet compounds also indicates that the interaction changes with concentration. At higher ethanol concentrations, sweetness from sugars may be suppressed, while lower concentrations can enhance sweetness or have little effect.

For beverage progression, ABV therefore contributes directly to sensory composition. Increasing alcohol is not simply increasing intoxication potential; it may also change bitterness, sweetness, burn, warmth, and the overall balance of the beverage.
questions: How does repeated ethanol exposure affect sensitivity to alcohol burn across several courses?
Does oral irritation increase, decrease, or adapt during a long beverage progression?
How does ethanol interact with sweetness, bitterness, acidity, and spice in actual food pairings?
At what concentration does alcohol begin to dominate rather than support a pairing?

revisions.title: Genre labels for Emperor’s Earth
revisions.content: Emperor’s Earth is primarily present-day speculative science fiction, with strong elements of alien-contact apocalyptic fiction, post-apocalyptic survival science fiction, and philosophical and psychological science fiction.

snapshot.title: Genre labels for Emperor’s Earth
snapshot.mainIdea: Emperor’s Earth is primarily present-day speculative science fiction, with strong elements of alien-contact apocalyptic fiction, post-apocalyptic survival science fiction, and philosophical and psychological science fiction.
snapshot.body:
Primary Genre: Present-Day Speculative Science Fiction

Emperor’s Earth is set within recognizable present-day geography and history, but the ordinary world is altered through alien contact, extraordinary powers, survival systems, advanced technology, and consequences that extend beyond Earth.

The story uses real locations such as Caton Avenue, Ocean Avenue, Prospect Park, Rikers Island, the Pulaski Skyway, Route 22, and Plainfield. These familiar settings ground the story in a recognizable world while the Mirrian attack and Kido’s transformation break that reality open. The manuscript follows Kido and Ricky from Rikers Island toward Plainfield through these identifiable locations.

Strong Secondary Genre: Alien-Contact Apocalyptic Fiction

The Mirrians and humanity initially exist within a peaceful relationship, but that relationship collapses after the Mirrians discover concealed acts committed by humanity. The resulting attack devastates Earth and leaves only part of its population alive.

The story is therefore not only about aliens existing or arriving. It examines the destruction that follows failed contact and the question of why peace became “Na-Ja-Jorel”—no peace. The manuscript connects the attack to the Mirrians’ discovery of humanity’s hidden violence and exploitation of another alien species.

Another Accurate Label: Post-Apocalyptic Survival Science Fiction

After the Mirrian attack, survival and rebuilding become central to the story.

Kido searches for people he loves, frees Ricky from Rikers Island, finds shelter, helps survivors, and becomes involved in building systems for food, medical care, communication, protection, and recovery.

The story moves beyond surviving the initial attack. It also examines how people organize, rebuild community, and determine what kind of society will follow the collapse.

Deeper Thematic Label: Philosophical and Psychological Science Fiction

The story is not only about aliens, powers, or destruction. It examines peace and control, trauma, responsibility, manipulation, moral collapse, abuse of power, identity, and the consequences of using power without restraint.

The conflict between Kido and Doctor Feldman establishes this structure. Kido struggles with responsibility, trauma, leadership, and the possibility of becoming either a protector or a destroyer. Feldman pursues control through manipulation, experimentation, and programming.

Kido’s conflict is also internal. The manuscript presents a struggle between the person he understands himself to be and the entity or power developing within him.

These labels are not competing classifications. They describe different levels of the same work:

  • Present-day speculative science fiction identifies the broad primary genre.

  • Alien-contact apocalyptic fiction identifies the event that breaks the ordinary world.

  • Post-apocalyptic survival science fiction identifies the survival and rebuilding structure.

  • Philosophical and psychological science fiction identifies the deeper moral and internal concerns

Recipe Name: Golden Coconut Curry–Roasted Brussels Sprouts and Creamer Potatoes
Cuisine: Indian-Inspired American
Course: Main Course or Side Dish
Category: Roasted Vegetables
Dietary Considerations: Vegan, Vegetarian, Dairy-Free
Yield: 6 servings

Flavor Profile:
Taste: Savory, mildly sweet, warmly spiced, and lightly salty
Aroma: Toasted coconut, turmeric, roasted onion, and caramelized vegetables
Mouthfeel: Crisp-edged Brussels sprouts, creamy potatoes, and a rich curry coating

🧠 General Description:

A high-temperature convection-roasted vegetable dish featuring tender yellow creamer potatoes, caramelized shredded Brussels sprouts, dehydrated onion, sweet pepper, and Brooklyn Delhi Golden Coconut Curry sauce. The sauce adds coconut richness, ginger, turmeric, lemon, and gentle warming spices.

💵 Suggested Price:

$9.00 per serving as a vegetable entrée or $6.00 per serving as a shared side dish.

📋 Menu Description:

Crispy Brussels sprouts and creamy yellow potatoes roasted with golden coconut curry, sweet peppers, onion, and aromatic spices.

🌍 Origins

This dish combines Indian-inspired coconut curry flavors with the Western technique of high-temperature sheet-pan roasting. Coconut-based curries are common throughout southern India and neighboring regions, while roasted Brussels sprouts and creamer potatoes reflect contemporary American vegetable cookery.

📜 History

Coconut, turmeric, ginger, onion, and aromatic spices have long been used in regional South Asian cooking. Prepared simmer sauces translate these established flavor combinations into convenient modern formats. Roasting the sauce with vegetables concentrates its flavors and creates caramelized edges that differ from the softer consistency of a traditionally simmered curry.

Cultural Significance

The recipe represents a contemporary fusion approach in which traditional South Asian flavor profiles are applied to readily available vegetables and modern convection-oven techniques. It also demonstrates how a prepared curry sauce can serve as both a seasoning and a roasting glaze.

🔪 Techniques

  • High-temperature convection roasting

  • Par-cooking potatoes for even doneness

  • Rehydrating dried vegetables

  • Tossing and coating

  • Sheet-pan spacing

  • Mid-roast turning

  • Resting before service

🛠️ Equipment

  • Convection oven

  • Large rimmed sheet pan

  • Parchment paper or silicone baking mat

  • Large mixing bowl

  • Small heat-resistant bowl

  • Colander

  • Measuring cups

  • Measuring spoons

  • Chef’s knife

  • Cutting board

  • Flexible spatula

  • Instant-read thermometer

🧯 HACCP Table

HACCP Code #DescriptionHACCP-1Wash hands, sanitize equipment, and inspect the Brussels sprouts and potatoes before preparation.HACCP-2Prevent cross-contamination by using clean utensils, bowls, and cutting surfaces.HACCP-3Roast the vegetables until the potatoes are tender and the dish reaches at least 165°F (74°C) before service.HACCP-4Hold the finished dish at 135°F (57°C) or above when it is not served immediately.HACCP-5Cool leftovers from 135°F to 70°F (57°C to 21°C) within 2 hours and from 70°F to 41°F (21°C to 5°C) within an additional 4 hours.HACCP-6Refrigerate opened curry sauce and cooked leftovers at 41°F (5°C) or below.

CCP Table

🧾 Ingredients

ImperialMetricIngredientPreparationTime1 bag, 1.5 lb680 gLittle Potato Company Little Yellows Fresh Creamer PotatoesWashed, drained, and halved if large5 minutes1 package, 10 oz284 gShredded Brussels sproutsInspected and separated2 minutes1/4 cup60 mLBrooklyn Delhi Golden Coconut Curry Simmer SauceStirred before measuring1 minute2 tablespoons30 mLOlive oilDivided1 minute1/4 cup20 gDehydrated onionRehydrated and drained10 minutes1/3 cup25 gDehydrated sweet pepperRehydrated and drained10 minutesTo tasteTo tasteSaltAdded gradually1 minuteTo tasteTo tasteBlack pepperFreshly ground if available1 minute

📖 Instructions

  1. Preheat a convection oven to 450°F (232°C). Position a rack in the center of the oven and line a large rimmed sheet pan with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

  2. Place the dehydrated onion and dehydrated sweet pepper in a heat-resistant bowl. Cover them with hot water and allow them to rehydrate for 10 minutes. Drain thoroughly and press out excess water.

  3. Wash and inspect the creamer potatoes. Halve any potatoes that are larger than approximately 1 inch (2.5 cm) in diameter so the pieces cook evenly.

  4. Place the potatoes in a microwave-safe covered container with 2 tablespoons (30 mL) water. Microwave for 5 to 7 minutes, or until slightly tender but not fully cooked. Drain well. Alternatively, simmer them in water for 8 to 10 minutes and drain thoroughly.

  5. Combine the par-cooked potatoes, shredded Brussels sprouts, rehydrated onion, rehydrated sweet pepper, olive oil, salt, and black pepper in a large mixing bowl.

  6. Add the Golden Coconut Curry Simmer Sauce and toss until the vegetables are evenly coated.

  7. Spread the mixture across the prepared sheet pan in a shallow, even layer. Turn the potatoes cut-side down and avoid overcrowding the Brussels sprouts.

  8. Roast at 450°F (232°C) on convection for 15 minutes.

  9. Remove the pan from the oven and turn the potatoes and Brussels sprouts with a flexible spatula. Redistribute any vegetables that are browning more quickly around the edges.

  10. Return the pan to the oven and roast for an additional 12 to 15 minutes, until the potatoes are tender, the Brussels sprouts have crisp caramelized edges, and the sauce is concentrated around the vegetables.

  11. Confirm that the center of the dish has reached at least 165°F (74°C). Remove the sheet pan from the oven.

  12. Taste and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper as needed.

  13. Allow the vegetables to rest on the sheet pan for 5 minutes so the curry coating thickens slightly and adheres to the vegetables.

  14. Transfer to a warmed serving platter or portion directly onto individual plates. Serve immediately.

🍽️ Plating:

Arrange the potatoes through the center of a shallow warmed bowl and mound the roasted Brussels sprouts over and around them. Spoon any concentrated curry mixture from the sheet pan over the vegetables. Finish with freshly ground black pepper. For added color, garnish with fresh cilantro or thinly sliced scallions when available.

📝 Notes

  • Par-cooking the potatoes helps them become creamy inside during the same roasting time required to caramelize the shredded Brussels sprouts.

  • Drain the rehydrated onion and peppers thoroughly. Excess water can steam the vegetables and reduce browning.

  • Use a sufficiently large sheet pan. Overcrowding traps moisture and produces softer vegetables.

  • The curry sauce contains coconut cream, ginger, turmeric, lemon, onion, garlic, and spices, giving the dish richness and mild aromatic heat.

  • The nutritional estimate assumes six servings and approximately 1 teaspoon of added salt for the complete recipe.

  • The stated ingredient cost is approximately $15.98 before accounting for salt, pepper, and any delivery charges.

🧊 Storage:

Cool leftovers promptly in shallow containers. Refrigerate at 41°F (5°C) or below for up to 4 days. Reheat uncovered in a 400°F (204°C) convection oven for 8 to 12 minutes, or until the center reaches 165°F (74°C). The dish may be frozen for up to 2 months, although the Brussels sprouts and potatoes may soften after thawing.

revisions.title: Two Versions of History
revisions.content: There are two parallel visions of history. One is the truth of what happened. The other is “his-story,” the version created by the conqueror or by the person telling the story. The idea explores how both versions can exist beside each other, while the version preserved by power becomes the history people accept.

snapshot.title: Two Versions of History
snapshot.mainIdea: There are two parallel visions of history. One is the truth of what happened. The other is “his-story,” the version created by the conqueror or by the person telling the story. The idea explores how both versions can exist beside each other, while the version preserved by power becomes the history people accept.
snapshot.body:
Two visions of the same history can exist in parallel. One is the truth of what happened. The other is the account created by the person or group controlling how the event is told, recorded, preserved, and taught.

“His-story” represents the conceptual division between an event and the account constructed from it. The accepted account may contain truth, omission, distortion, interpretation, or deliberate invention. Although multiple versions may continue to exist, only one may be granted public authority.

The conqueror or dominant group may control books, education, monuments, archives, language, and public ceremonies. The defeated or excluded may preserve their version through oral history, private records, art, ritual, and family memory.

Neither version is automatically complete. Each side may possess fragments of the truth, and memory may alter an account even when the person telling it intends to be honest. The central tension is not simply between truth and falsehood, but between what happened, what was remembered, what was recorded, and what survived with enough authority to be called history.

revisions.title: Mount Gay Rum
revisions.content:
Mount Gay presents Barbados and its rum-making tradition as inseparable, shaped by the island’s geology, culture, landscape, and centuries of craftsmanship.

Water
Mount Gay uses water from a deep artesian well located on its original property in Saint Lucy, Barbados. The well was first dug in 1703 and remains in use. The water rises from coral caverns hundreds of feet underground and is naturally filtered through the island’s coral geology.

Yeast and Fermentation
Yeast converts the sugars in molasses into alcohol during fermentation. Mount Gay uses two fermentation methods.

Closed fermentation is used for column distillation and uses a proprietary heirloom yeast strain developed by Mount Gay’s rum makers.

Open-air fermentation is used for pot-still distillation. The molasses-and-water mixture is exposed to the Barbadian environment, allowing native airborne yeasts to enter the fermentation and contribute to the rum’s aromatic character.

Molasses
Mount Gay uses molasses produced from selected Barbadian and Caribbean sugarcane. The molasses has a malty character with notes of caramel and toffee, along with acidity and slight bitterness in the finish.

Key Significance
The character of Mount Gay rum is connected to Barbados through its water, native yeasts, sugarcane, climate, geology, and traditional production methods.

zettelIds.title: Mirrinese Lexicon
zettelIds.mainIdea:
Core Roots

ja-jorel — peace; state of harmonious stillness; also used as a personal name.

lin — light; illumination; associated with First Rise.

len — sustain; foundational root for nourishment and vitality.

hal — food; sustenance; tied to offerings and daily provision.

ra — give; provide; offer.

sha — expression of gratitude; used in formal thanks.

va — our; collective belonging.

no — my; individual affirmation.

sa — nourish; restore; used in blessings.

vash — until; up to a future meeting or moment; temporal marker of continuation.

 

Compound Forms (Derived from Roots)

Ha’lin — to greet the light; morning acknowledgment.

Shalen — we thank; communal gratitude.

Ven-hal — for the food; gratitude for sustenance.

No’reth — that which you provide; offering or gift.

Sa’len — nourish; restore our being.

Va-lin — our being; shared essence.

Prayer (Mirrinese + English)

Ha’lin ja-jorel.

We greet the light in peace.

Mirria, shalen ven-hal no’reth to-ra.

Mirria, we thank you for the food you provide.

Sa’len va-lin.

Nourish our being.

KIDO’S TABLET NOTES — WHAT EARTH MUST BUILD GOING FORWARD

(This is the REAL list you were asking for — the actionable future work.)

1. A global transparency framework

– no secret programs

– no hidden labs

– no unilateral decisions

– mandatory disclosure rules

 2. A planetary ethics board independent of government

– can veto experiments

– can halt research instantly

– protects biological life (human + non-human)

3. Reconstruction of leadership structures

– remove military-first decision models

– civilian oversight

– remove anyone tied to old abuses

– establish clear chains of accountability

4. A unified education initiative

– teach the real history (genocide, misuse of tech)

– teach Mirrian principles of balance/respect

– dismantle the aggressive worldview that caused Na Ja-Jorel

 5. A technology-governance charter

– rules for developing, testing, and storing any advanced tech

– mandatory fail-safes

– restrictions on energy-based weapons or manipulation systems

6. A planetary council of nations

– replaces secret coalitions

– open decision-making

– one global body to prevent individual nations from going rogue

7. A new conflict-resolution system

– early-warning mechanisms

– mediation teams

– no escalation without planetary approval

 8. A scientific oversight alliance

– independent review of any genetic or technological research

– cross-examination from multiple fields

– no single scientist or agency can steer humanity

9. Survivor support and stabilization

– mental health framework

– rebuilding housing

– restoring lost communities

– foundations for long-term cultural stability

 

10. A planetary value statement

– respect for life

– no subjugation, no domination

– no exploitation of other species

– stewardship of power

 

11. A long-term evolution plan

– benchmarks for maturity

– social, technological, and ethical milestones

– periodic self-audit to track growth

 

12. A blueprint for interspecies relationships

– guidelines for respecting other civilizations

– rules for exchange, communication, and shared technology

– protocols for accountability if Earth slips again

 

13. Kido’s internal responsibilities

– maintain balance between power and restraint

– create a successor structure not dependent on him

– train others to act as guardians of the new system

revisions.title: Petrichor
revisions.content:
Petrichor


Darrell Barrow
© 8/7/2026

The dryness.
The dirt—
Agh!
Look at the grass.

The yard.
Cross slowly,
the grass thins down to dirt in places,
wherever the green has dried out.

Look up.
The sky.
The blue is gone.
Clouds moving in.

Then—
A drop.
Dark on the ground.
Then a few more, sparse.

From the dark spots,
something rises;
the air changes.

Fresh,
Cool,
Clean,
Invigorating.

Leaves brighten and lift.
Dust settles.
Stones darken.
Green slowly returns.

The rain is harder now.
Run for the house.
Stand in the doorway.
Watch the falling rain.

You smile.
One less chore for the day.
Water the yard—
Checked.
Mother Nature lent a hand.

Breathe in.
Stay in the doorway.
Just a little longer.
Nothing needs doing.
Neither do you.

The rain stops.
Breathe in.
Something remains.
Still there.

revisions.title: Shotgun Squirrel
revisions.content:
Shotgun Squirrel

Darrell Barrow
© 7/30/2026

I watch a squirrel I named "Carl."
He keeps count of everything.
Every nut,
every French fry,
every seed collected from the pavement.

He would greet me
as I sat on my favorite bench
with a McChicken, fries, and vanilla iced coffee.

I would watch him scurry behind me,
occasionally looking at me as we ate.
He would pause beside the bench.
"Good afternoon," I said
as I took a bite of a French fry.

He stood, looking across the ground.
I asked,
"Would you like some fries with that?"
I chuckled to myself,
pulling out a fry and tossing it his way.
Carl looked at the fry,
picked it up, and ate it.
"Would you like some ketchup with your fries?"
I said.

Carl would visit almost every day.
We exchanged looks
as we went about our routine.
We ate,
and he would pause on either side of me.

I'd break off a piece of my McChicken
and toss it his way.
He would grab it.
"Sorry, I have no French fries today."

"Would you like some for later?
Winter is coming,
and I know you have to prepare."

I prepared each day,
expecting to see Carl.
French fries, vanilla coffee,
and a McChicken.
I wonder if Carl is sad
on the days I don't show.

On one particular day,
Carl was heading my way.
I tossed a French fry in his direction.
A bird swooped down
and grabbed it.

Carl stopped,
sat back on his hind legs,
looked at me,
then at the bird.
He pulled out a shotgun,
shot the bird,
put it away,
then continued toward his fry.

I will never look at Carl the same again.
My "Shotgun Squirrel."

revisions.title: The View From Here
revisions.content:
The View From Here


Darrell Barrow
© 7/23/2026

You offer a destination,
but will I walk the path?

From here, it looks like peace,
but images can be deceiving.

You show everything I want
But will it be what I need?

What lies beyond what I can see?
I fear what I may find:
peace,
terror.
My mind wanders.

Should I trust your apparent relief?
It's wrong to judge you from what I feel.
Trust does not come easy for me.

You answer with a sea-filled gentle breeze.
Are you tempting me?
What are you trying to offer me?

Am I too hurt to see
your offer of peace,
solitude, and relief?

You answer,
in a gentle wave of palm leaves.
Are you responding to me?
Do you know the real me?
The me reluctant to accept your invitation of peace?

Ocean of blue
Sand tan
The sun low,
like a northern star.
I see solitude and peace,
but these questions lie beneath.

You answer by parting a palm tree.
The sun reflects wholly on me.
A peaceful, serene stage.
Sun rays tightly spotted on me.

I take a step,
the sun's rays energizing me.
You answer with a gentle breeze.

Take a few more steps.
The sun's rays ripple through the leaves.
Silhouettes caress my face.

I turn to see I have walked further than I thought.
Halfway between here and where.
Here is different from where I was.
You answer with the smell of the sea.

Why did I ever doubt?
You seem to know me.
A hermit crab greets me,
turns, and leads the way.

It waits at the end to the side,
Waiting—
I pause before the sand
the sun full on my face.
I look at the crab and smile
as he turns and goes his way.

I turn to the left.
A table with an umbrella and a chair greets me.
It seems you are expecting me.
You answer, showering the table in palm leaves.

Birds fly in formation toward the setting set for me,
circling the table
as if saying, "Have a seat."

Okay, I get it. This is for me.
I remove my shoes;
my feet touch the sand.
Perfectly warmed to soothe my tired feet.
I whisper, "Thank you. You did all this for me."

I move toward the seat while
the sun bathes me in warmth.
I tip my hat in thanks.

At the table, before I sit,
what do I see?
A fresh coconut lying, waiting for me.
A rock perfectly placed.
I crack open the shell,
careful not to spill its water.
I take a sip as I sit in the chair.
I set the other half aside for you.
My personal thank you.

You reply with a brisk ocean breeze.
Raising my coconut,
I toast the wind.

I embrace the warmth of the sun.
I accept the scent of the sea.
I find relief in the coolness of the breeze.
I play with the sand beneath my feet.
I gently talk to the palm trees.
Thank you all for making this space for me.

The hours pass.
The sun lowers its head.
A gull passes overhead,
drops a fish,
leaves; there is nothing to be said.
Thank you, Mr. Gull.
Now I'm even fed.

The sun yawns as it readies for bed.
I get up, find a leaf, and wrap my fish.
I head back to the path.
It's different now.

Why did I question?
Why did I hesitate?
Why did I fear?

I look back from whence I came.
Life was there,
but now reframed.


Author’s Note

This poem began during a therapy session while I was discussing deeply buried emotional experiences. During a pause in the conversation, I looked at a calendar image behind my therapist. The path stood out to me first, and I said that the image was speaking to me and that I needed to write about it.

I did not plan the poem or decide beforehand what the image should mean. I looked at the scene and allowed it to lead me. As I entered the image in my mind, the landscape responded through sunlight, wind, palm leaves, animals, and the sea.

I have always been drawn to nature, solitude, and the things that can happen when we become quiet enough to listen. For me, this poem became an experience of finding peace and gaining a different perspective on the difficulties I have encountered over time.

snapshot.title: The View From Here
snapshot.description: A reflective poem inspired by an image of a weathered wooden path leading through beach grass and palm trees toward the ocean at sunset. The speaker studies the path with hesitation, questioning whether the peace it appears to offer can be trusted. As the landscape responds through sunlight, wind, leaves, animals, sand, and sea, the speaker gradually moves forward, accepts the invitation to rest, and gains a changed perspective on the life left behind.

zettelIds.title: Mirrinese Lexicon
zettelIds.mainIdea:
Core Roots

ja-jorel — peace; state of harmonious stillness; also used as a personal name.

lin — light; illumination; associated with First Rise.

len — sustain; foundational root for nourishment and vitality.

hal — food; sustenance; tied to offerings and daily provision.

ra — give; provide; offer.

sha — expression of gratitude; used in formal thanks.

va — our; collective belonging.

no — my; individual affirmation.

sa — nourish; restore; used in blessings.

vash — until; up to a future meeting or moment; temporal marker of continuation.

 

Compound Forms (Derived from Roots)

Ha’lin — to greet the light; morning acknowledgment.

Shalen — we thank; communal gratitude.

Ven-hal — for the food; gratitude for sustenance.

No’reth — that which you provide; offering or gift.

Sa’len — nourish; restore our being.

Va-lin — our being; shared essence.

Prayer (Mirrinese + English)

Ha’lin ja-jorel.

We greet the light in peace.

Mirria, shalen ven-hal no’reth to-ra.

Mirria, we thank you for the food you provide.

Sa’len va-lin.

Nourish our being.

KIDO’S TABLET NOTES — WHAT EARTH MUST BUILD GOING FORWARD

(This is the REAL list you were asking for — the actionable future work.)

1. A global transparency framework

– no secret programs

– no hidden labs

– no unilateral decisions

– mandatory disclosure rules

 2. A planetary ethics board independent of government

– can veto experiments

– can halt research instantly

– protects biological life (human + non-human)

3. Reconstruction of leadership structures

– remove military-first decision models

– civilian oversight

– remove anyone tied to old abuses

– establish clear chains of accountability

4. A unified education initiative

– teach the real history (genocide, misuse of tech)

– teach Mirrian principles of balance/respect

– dismantle the aggressive worldview that caused Na Ja-Jorel

 5. A technology-governance charter

– rules for developing, testing, and storing any advanced tech

– mandatory fail-safes

– restrictions on energy-based weapons or manipulation systems

6. A planetary council of nations

– replaces secret coalitions

– open decision-making

– one global body to prevent individual nations from going rogue

7. A new conflict-resolution system

– early-warning mechanisms

– mediation teams

– no escalation without planetary approval

 8. A scientific oversight alliance

– independent review of any genetic or technological research

– cross-examination from multiple fields

– no single scientist or agency can steer humanity

9. Survivor support and stabilization

– mental health framework

– rebuilding housing

– restoring lost communities

– foundations for long-term cultural stability

 

10. A planetary value statement

– respect for life

– no subjugation, no domination

– no exploitation of other species

– stewardship of power

 

11. A long-term evolution plan

– benchmarks for maturity

– social, technological, and ethical milestones

– periodic self-audit to track growth

 

12. A blueprint for interspecies relationships

– guidelines for respecting other civilizations

– rules for exchange, communication, and shared technology

– protocols for accountability if Earth slips again

 

13. Kido’s internal responsibilities

– maintain balance between power and restraint

– create a successor structure not dependent on him

– train others to act as guardians of the new system

revisions.title: Bajan and Japanese Cuisines Share Flavor Philosophies but Express Them Differently
revisions.content: Bajan and Japanese cuisines can share similar flavor philosophies while expressing those ideas through different ingredients, techniques, and cultural traditions.

snapshot.title: Bajan and Japanese Cuisines Share Flavor Philosophies but Express Them Differently
snapshot.mainIdea: Bajan and Japanese cuisines can share similar flavor philosophies while expressing those ideas through different ingredients, techniques, and cultural traditions.
snapshot.body:
The connection between Bajan and Japanese cuisine is not that the cuisines taste the same. The connection is that they can approach flavor through similar underlying principles while producing different results.

Both cuisines value balance, depth, seasoning, freshness, and the careful use of ingredients. Their expressions differ because each cuisine is shaped by its own culture, environment, available ingredients, history, and cooking methods.

This shared philosophy provides a reason to explore Bajan and Japanese cuisines together without treating either as interchangeable with the other.

revisions.title: Culinary Experimentation
revisions.content: Culinary experimentation is a structured process of testing ingredients, techniques, proportions, and ideas to discover how they affect a dish.

snapshot.title: Culinary Experimentation
snapshot.mainIdea: Culinary experimentation is a structured process of testing ingredients, techniques, proportions, and ideas to discover how they affect a dish.
snapshot.body:
Culinary experimentation allows ideas to be tested rather than accepted only in theory. An experiment may examine an ingredient pairing, cooking method, seasoning level, texture, temperature, substitution, or presentation.

Useful experimentation requires a clear purpose. Changing too many variables at once can make it difficult to understand what caused the result. Testing one major change at a time can produce more useful observations.

The outcome does not need to be successful to have value. An unsuccessful test can reveal problems with proportion, technique, timing, balance, or the original assumption. Recording observations makes the experiment useful for future recipe development and prevents the same test from being repeated without learning.

revisions.title: Desired Profit Determines Ideal Expense
revisions.content: Profit should be planned in advance rather than treated as whatever remains after expenses are paid.

snapshot.title: Desired Profit Determines Ideal Expense
snapshot.mainIdea: Profit should be planned in advance rather than treated as whatever remains after expenses are paid.
snapshot.body:
An appropriate level of business profit results from solid planning, management, and careful decision-making. Profit should not be viewed simply as money left over after all bills have been paid. Earning profit requires deliberate preplanning.

Because business owners and investors accept financial risk, the operation must plan for a level of profit that makes that investment worthwhile. A restaurant may be capable of generating profit, but profitability is not guaranteed.

The modified profit formula recognizes profit as a planned financial objective:

Revenue − Desired Profit = Ideal Expense

Desired profit is established first. The amount remaining after subtracting desired profit from expected revenue represents the ideal level of expense the operation can incur while still achieving its profit objective.

This shifts management thinking from:

Revenue − Expenses = Whatever Profit Remains

to:

Expected Revenue − Planned Profit = Allowable Expense

The principle is that management should control expenses in relation to a predetermined profit goal rather than allowing expenses to occur first and accepting whatever profit remains afterward.

revisions.title: Hebrew Three Watches of the Night
revisions.content: In the Hebrew three-watch system, the night was divided into three approximate four-hour periods: evening, midnight, and morning.

snapshot.title: Hebrew Three Watches of the Night
snapshot.mainIdea: In the Hebrew three-watch system, the night was divided into three approximate four-hour periods: evening, midnight, and morning.
snapshot.body:
First Watch — Evening:
Approximately 6 PM–10 PM.

The first watch covered the early portion of the night.

Psalm 63:6 refers generally to meditating during the watches of the night.

Second Watch — Midnight:
Approximately 10 PM–2 AM.

Judges 7:19 refers to Gideon reaching the camp at the beginning of the middle watch.

Third Watch — Morning:
Approximately 2 AM–6 AM.

The morning watch covered the final portion of the night approaching dawn.

Psalm 119:147 describes rising before dawn and crying for help.

The clock times assigned to the three watches are approximate historical divisions rather than exact times stated in the biblical text.

revisions.title: Hellenistic and Roman Four Watches of the Night
revisions.content: In the Hellenistic and Roman four-watch system, the night was divided into four approximate three-hour periods: evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning.

snapshot.title: Hellenistic and Roman Four Watches of the Night
snapshot.mainIdea: In the Hellenistic and Roman four-watch system, the night was divided into four approximate three-hour periods: evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning.
snapshot.body:
First Watch — Evening:
Approximately 6 PM–9 PM.

This was the first portion of the night after sunset.

Second Watch — Midnight:
Approximately 9 PM–12 AM.

This watch extended through the period approaching midnight.

Third Watch — Cockcrow:
Approximately 12 AM–3 AM.

This watch covered the period after midnight and before the final watch of the night.

Fourth Watch — Morning:
Approximately 3 AM–6 AM.

Matthew 14:25 places Jesus approaching the disciples during the fourth watch of the night.

Mark 13:35 presents four divisions of the night using the terms evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning.

The four-watch system divided an approximately twelve-hour night into four periods of roughly three hours each.

revisions.title: Four Categories of Food Hazards
revisions.content: A food hazard is any substance in food capable of causing illness or injury, and food hazards are classified as biological, chemical, physical, or allergenic.

snapshot.title: Four Categories of Food Hazards
snapshot.mainIdea: A food hazard is any substance in food capable of causing illness or injury, and food hazards are classified as biological, chemical, physical, or allergenic.
snapshot.body:
Food contamination occurs when food contains harmful substances that were not originally present. A hazard is any substance in food capable of causing illness or injury.

The four categories of food hazards are:

  • Biological hazards

  • Chemical hazards

  • Physical hazards

  • Allergens

Not every food hazard results from contamination. Some hazards occur naturally in foods, including plant toxins, seafood toxins, and naturally occurring substances that trigger allergic reactions. This distinction means food-safety controls must address both introduced contaminants and hazards inherent to particular foods.

revisions.title: Pathogens as Biological Hazards
revisions.content: A pathogen is a disease-causing microorganism, and food can contain dangerous pathogens without showing visible signs of contamination.

snapshot.title: Pathogens as Biological Hazards
snapshot.mainIdea: A pathogen is a disease-causing microorganism, and food can contain dangerous pathogens without showing visible signs of contamination.
snapshot.body:
Microorganisms are tiny organisms generally visible only through a microscope. A microorganism capable of causing disease is called a pathogen.

Four groups of microorganisms can contaminate food and cause illness:

  • Bacteria

  • Viruses

  • Fungi

  • Parasites

Their microscopic nature creates an important food-safety problem: contaminated food may appear normal. Visual appearance alone therefore cannot establish whether food is microbiologically safe.

Bacteria cause many foodborne diseases and consequently receive significant attention in sanitation practices, although controls that protect food against bacteria can also help prevent contamination by other microorganisms.

sourceIds.title: Professional Cooking

questions: Which preventive controls work across multiple pathogen types?
Which microorganisms require controls different from bacterial controls?

revisions.title: Practical Classification of Bacteria in Food Service
revisions.content: For food-service purposes, bacteria can be understood according to their practical effects as harmless, beneficial, undesirable, or disease-causing.

snapshot.title: Practical Classification of Bacteria in Food Service
snapshot.mainIdea: For food-service purposes, bacteria can be understood according to their practical effects as harmless, beneficial, undesirable, or disease-causing.
snapshot.body:
Bacteria occur throughout the environment and the human body. From a practical food-service perspective, they can be grouped according to their effects.

Harmless bacteria neither benefit nor harm humans and are generally not a sanitation concern.

Beneficial bacteria perform useful functions, including supporting digestion and enabling production of foods such as cheese, yogurt, and sauerkraut.

Undesirable bacteria cause food spoilage, including souring, decomposition, slime, discoloration, and objectionable odors. Spoilage causes financial loss and can indicate improper handling or storage.

Disease-causing bacteria are pathogens responsible for foodborne illness.

An important distinction is that spoilage organisms may announce themselves through sensory changes, while pathogenic bacteria may not.

revisions.title: Yield Percentage
revisions.content: Yield percentage expresses the usable portion of an ingredient as a percentage of its original as-purchased quantity.

snapshot.title: Yield Percentage
snapshot.mainIdea: Yield percentage expresses the usable portion of an ingredient as a percentage of its original as-purchased quantity.
snapshot.body:
Yield percentage compares edible-portion quantity with as-purchased quantity. It shows how much of the purchased product remains usable after trimming, cleaning, fabrication, cooking, or other losses.

A higher yield percentage means that more of the purchased ingredient remains available for use. A lower yield percentage indicates greater loss, although a lower yield does not automatically mean the ingredient is a poor purchase. Product quality, purchase price, labor requirements, flavor, and the value of usable trim must also be considered.

Yield percentage can support purchasing calculations, cost comparisons, recipe costing, waste analysis, and production planning. Actual kitchen testing may be necessary because published percentages do not account for every product, supplier, or preparation standard.

Calculation

Yield Percentage = Edible-Portion Quantity ÷ As-Purchased Quantity × 100

revisions.title: I Built the Dungeon That Killed Me
revisions.content: The book title "I Built the Dungeon That Killed Me" inspired an idea for a poem. The central premise is that the speaker has constructed the very thing that ultimately confines or destroys them. The dungeon is built gradually, through choices, habits, actions, or repeated acts whose consequences may not be understood while they are happening. A central tension is: if I built the dungeon myself, why can't I leave it? The poem could allow that question to remain unanswered.

revisions.title: Acid as a foundational element of cooking
revisions.content: Acid creates brightness, contrast, structure, and balance while changing how salt, sweetness, bitterness, richness, and other flavors are perceived.

snapshot.title: Acid as a foundational element of cooking
snapshot.mainIdea: Acid creates brightness, contrast, structure, and balance while changing how salt, sweetness, bitterness, richness, and other flavors are perceived.
snapshot.body:
Acid can brighten a dish, balance richness, sharpen indistinct flavors, and create contrast. It may come from citrus, vinegar, fermented ingredients, cultured dairy, fruit, wine, tomatoes, or other acidic foods.

Different acids have distinct flavors and intensities. They should therefore be selected according to the ingredients, cooking method, and intended character of the dish.

Acid can be introduced during cooking or used as a finishing element. Its timing affects whether it becomes integrated, softened, concentrated, or clearly noticeable. The purpose is not simply to make food sour, but to create balance and definition.

revisions.title: Fat as a foundational element of cooking
revisions.content: Fat carries flavor, creates texture, transfers heat, adds richness, and shapes how a dish feels and tastes.

snapshot.title: Fat as a foundational element of cooking
snapshot.mainIdea: Fat carries flavor, creates texture, transfers heat, adds richness, and shapes how a dish feels and tastes.
snapshot.body:
Fat performs several culinary functions. It can carry aromatic compounds, provide richness, affect tenderness, create crispness, produce emulsions, and transfer heat during cooking.

Different fats contribute different flavors and behave differently under heat. Butter, olive oil, coconut milk, animal fats, seed oils, dairy, nuts, and other fat sources cannot always be treated as interchangeable.

The amount and type of fat should support the purpose of the dish. Too little may leave a dish dry, thin, or incomplete. Too much may suppress clarity or make the dish feel heavy. Acid, salt, heat, texture, and moisture can affect how richness is perceived.

snapshot.title: Aromatic compounds in cooking
snapshot.mainIdea: Aromatic compounds contribute to how ingredients smell and taste, and understanding their relationships can support ingredient pairing and flavor development.
snapshot.body:
Aroma forms a major part of flavor perception. Ingredients contain volatile aromatic compounds that are released, altered, concentrated, or lost through cutting, crushing, heating, fermenting, drying, and other culinary processes.

Ingredients that share certain aromatic compounds may form useful pairings, but shared compounds do not guarantee that a combination will work. Taste, texture, intensity, preparation, cultural context, and the overall structure of the dish remain important.

Aromatic-compound information can be used as a tool for exploration. It may suggest unexpected ingredient relationships or help explain familiar combinations, but the final decision must still be tested through cooking and tasting.

zettelIds.title: Mirrinese Lexicon
zettelIds.mainIdea:
Core Roots

ja-jorel — peace; state of harmonious stillness; also used as a personal name.

lin — light; illumination; associated with First Rise.

len — sustain; foundational root for nourishment and vitality.

hal — food; sustenance; tied to offerings and daily provision.

ra — give; provide; offer.

sha — expression of gratitude; used in formal thanks.

va — our; collective belonging.

no — my; individual affirmation.

sa — nourish; restore; used in blessings.

vash — until; up to a future meeting or moment; temporal marker of continuation.

 

Compound Forms (Derived from Roots)

Ha’lin — to greet the light; morning acknowledgment.

Shalen — we thank; communal gratitude.

Ven-hal — for the food; gratitude for sustenance.

No’reth — that which you provide; offering or gift.

Sa’len — nourish; restore our being.

Va-lin — our being; shared essence.

Prayer (Mirrinese + English)

Ha’lin ja-jorel.

We greet the light in peace.

Mirria, shalen ven-hal no’reth to-ra.

Mirria, we thank you for the food you provide.

Sa’len va-lin.

Nourish our being.

KIDO’S TABLET NOTES — WHAT EARTH MUST BUILD GOING FORWARD

(This is the REAL list you were asking for — the actionable future work.)

1. A global transparency framework

– no secret programs

– no hidden labs

– no unilateral decisions

– mandatory disclosure rules

 2. A planetary ethics board independent of government

– can veto experiments

– can halt research instantly

– protects biological life (human + non-human)

3. Reconstruction of leadership structures

– remove military-first decision models

– civilian oversight

– remove anyone tied to old abuses

– establish clear chains of accountability

4. A unified education initiative

– teach the real history (genocide, misuse of tech)

– teach Mirrian principles of balance/respect

– dismantle the aggressive worldview that caused Na Ja-Jorel

 5. A technology-governance charter

– rules for developing, testing, and storing any advanced tech

– mandatory fail-safes

– restrictions on energy-based weapons or manipulation systems

6. A planetary council of nations

– replaces secret coalitions

– open decision-making

– one global body to prevent individual nations from going rogue

7. A new conflict-resolution system

– early-warning mechanisms

– mediation teams

– no escalation without planetary approval

 8. A scientific oversight alliance

– independent review of any genetic or technological research

– cross-examination from multiple fields

– no single scientist or agency can steer humanity

9. Survivor support and stabilization

– mental health framework

– rebuilding housing

– restoring lost communities

– foundations for long-term cultural stability

 

10. A planetary value statement

– respect for life

– no subjugation, no domination

– no exploitation of other species

– stewardship of power

 

11. A long-term evolution plan

– benchmarks for maturity

– social, technological, and ethical milestones

– periodic self-audit to track growth

 

12. A blueprint for interspecies relationships

– guidelines for respecting other civilizations

– rules for exchange, communication, and shared technology

– protocols for accountability if Earth slips again

 

13. Kido’s internal responsibilities

– maintain balance between power and restraint

– create a successor structure not dependent on him

– train others to act as guardians of the new system

revisions.title: Emperor’s Earth
revisions.content:
Emperor’s Earth is a speculative-fiction manuscript centered on Kido Thompson after a Mirrian attack destroys much of Earth’s population. Kido survives and develops extraordinary abilities that place him between the possibility of becoming a protector and leader or becoming SHIVA, the destroyer of worlds.

The manuscript follows Kido’s relationships with Ricky Chapman, Kenji Nakamura, Mira Devereaux, Xavier, Ja-Jorel, and others as he struggles with trauma, responsibility, power, identity, manipulation, and rebuilding. Doctor Henry Feldman attempts to study, control, program, and use Kido through genetic research, behavioral manipulation, and ancient technology.

The story also involves The Order, the Russian Federation, Colonel Reed Hawkes, the Mirrians, political and military power, covert experimentation, alien contact, survival, reconciliation, and the ethical consequences of power. The manuscript includes twelve chapters, character profiles, organization profiles, Mirrian terminology, a working Mirrinese lexicon, and Kido’s notes concerning what Earth must build going forward.

snapshot.title: Emperor’s Earth organizations
snapshot.mainIdea: The organizations in Emperor’s Earth represent different forms of political, scientific, military, social, and extraterrestrial power, and their goals and relationships must remain clearly distinguished.
snapshot.body:
Emperor’s Earth contains several organizations and organized power structures that influence the plot.

The Order

A covert organization that provides Feldman with protection and resources. Its members pursue profit, political dominance, technological development, genetic enhancement, obedience, and social control.

Russian Federation

A political and military power with its own interest in Kido, Feldman’s research, genetic enhancement, strategic infiltration, and global dominance.

Its relationship with Feldman overlaps with The Order but also follows its own national agenda.

Kido’s Command Center

A survivor-led organization that develops from Kido’s former home. It coordinates communication, medical care, food, protection, scouting, research, and rebuilding after the attack.

The Mirrian High Council

The governing body involved in Mirrian political decisions, diplomacy, judgment, and the response to humanity’s actions.

The Mirrian Monarchy

Ka-Jorel and Ja-Jorel represent another form of Mirrian leadership that intersects with the High Council, Kido, and the relationship between Earth and Mirria.

Medical and scientific teams

Feldman’s medical team and associated researchers participate in testing, observation, manipulation, and reprogramming. Their individual knowledge, loyalty, and responsibility must be distinguished.

Military and security structures

Colonel Reed Hawkes and related personnel represent organized military or covert operations connected to capturing and controlling Kido.

Continuity concern

The manuscript uses both Society and The Order. This must be resolved so that readers can determine whether they are the same organization or separate organizations. Based on the developed chapters and profiles, The Order is the established name.

revisions.title: Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics
revisions.content: Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics are a fictional framework intended to control robot behavior by prioritizing human safety, obedience, and self-preservation, but conflicts between those priorities reveal the difficulty of reducing morality to fixed rules.

snapshot.title: Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics
snapshot.mainIdea: Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics are a fictional framework intended to control robot behavior by prioritizing human safety, obedience, and self-preservation, but conflicts between those priorities reveal the difficulty of reducing morality to fixed rules.
snapshot.body:
Isaac Asimov’s Three Laws of Robotics establish a hierarchy for robot behavior.

First Law

A robot must not harm a human being or knowingly allow a human being to be harmed through inaction.

Second Law

A robot must follow human instructions unless doing so would conflict with protecting a human being.

Third Law

A robot must protect its own existence as long as that protection does not conflict with human safety or human instructions.

The laws are hierarchical. Human safety takes priority over obedience, and obedience takes priority over a robot’s self-preservation.

Although the laws appear direct, their application creates uncertainty. A robot must interpret what counts as harm, determine whether action or inaction is more dangerous, decide which human instructions are legitimate, and predict the consequences of its choices.

The laws therefore do more than control robots. They create situations in which logic, language, incomplete knowledge, conflicting duties, and unintended consequences become central to the story.

Asimov used the laws as a framework for examining what happens when apparently clear rules encounter complicated human circumstances. The tension often comes not from a robot deliberately rejecting the laws, but from the different ways the laws can be interpreted or brought into conflict.

The laws are fictional and should not automatically be treated as a complete system for governing modern artificial intelligence. However, they remain useful for thinking about AI ethics, machine obedience, responsibility, safety, control, and the limits of rule-based morality.

revisions.title: Ratio: The Simple Codes Behind the Craft of Everyday Cooking
revisions.content:
Ratio presents foundational cooking preparations through proportional relationships between ingredients. Michael Ruhlman explains how understanding ratios can help cooks recognize the underlying structure of doughs, batters, custards, stocks, sauces, and other preparations.

The book emphasizes learning how ingredients function together rather than depending only on fixed recipes. By understanding the relationship between quantities, a cook can scale preparations, make substitutions, develop variations, troubleshoot results, and create new recipes with greater control. The book contains thirty-three culinary ratios and examples of how changing a ratio can transform one preparation into another.

revisions.title: Anatomy of a Craft Cocktail
revisions.content: A craft cocktail is defined by the intentional selection and combination of its elements rather than by complexity, specialized equipment, or elaborate technique.

snapshot.title: Anatomy of a Craft Cocktail
snapshot.mainIdea: A craft cocktail is defined by the intentional selection and combination of its elements rather than by complexity, specialized equipment, or elaborate technique.
snapshot.body:
A craft cocktail brings together spirits, mixers, garnishes, aroma, appearance, flavor, balance, mouthfeel, and presentation with deliberate care.

The quality of the drink comes from how well these individual elements work together. A successful craft cocktail should have visual appeal, an inviting aroma, balanced taste, depth of flavor, appropriate mouthfeel, and a distinctive character.

Craft does not necessarily mean complicated. Specialized equipment, advanced techniques, or elaborate preparation are not requirements. Creativity, thoughtful choices, quality ingredients, balance, and skill can produce a well-crafted drink without unnecessary complexity.

The description also adds another dimension to craft: story. A memorable cocktail may carry a history, inspiration, cultural connection, ingredient story, or other narrative that contributes to its identity.

The larger principle is that craft comes from intentionality. The finished product becomes more than its individual components because those components have been selected and assembled toward a coherent whole.

revisions.title: Bacteria Differ in Their Oxygen Requirements
revisions.content: The presence or absence of oxygen does not universally prevent bacterial growth because different bacteria have different oxygen requirements.

snapshot.title: Bacteria Differ in Their Oxygen Requirements
snapshot.mainIdea: The presence or absence of oxygen does not universally prevent bacterial growth because different bacteria have different oxygen requirements.
snapshot.body:
Bacteria can be classified according to their relationship with oxygen.

Aerobic bacteria require oxygen.

Anaerobic bacteria grow where oxygen is absent.

Facultative bacteria can grow with or without oxygen, and the chapter identifies most disease-causing food bacteria as facultative.

The absence of air therefore cannot automatically be treated as a food-safety control. In fact, oxygen-free environments can favor anaerobic pathogens. The chapter uses botulism as an important example of a disease caused by anaerobic bacteria

revisions.title: Bacteria Require a Vehicle for Transmission
revisions.content: Bacteria cannot independently travel through a kitchen; contamination occurs when people, food, equipment, water, air, pests, or other carriers move them.

snapshot.title: Bacteria Require a Vehicle for Transmission
snapshot.mainIdea: Bacteria cannot independently travel through a kitchen; contamination occurs when people, food, equipment, water, air, pests, or other carriers move them.
snapshot.body:
Bacteria move from one location to another only when something carries them.

Potential carriers identified in the chapter include:

  • Hands

  • Air

  • Coughs and sneezes

  • Water

  • Other foods

  • Insects

  • Equipment and utensils

  • Rats and mice

This principle shifts sanitation from merely killing microorganisms to controlling the pathways by which microorganisms reach food. Preventing contact between food and contaminated carriers is therefore a fundamental defense against foodborne illness.

revisions.title: Conditions Required for Bacterial Growth
revisions.content: Bacterial growth is controlled by environmental conditions including food, moisture, temperature, acidity, oxygen, and time.

snapshot.title: Conditions Required for Bacterial Growth
snapshot.mainIdea: Bacterial growth is controlled by environmental conditions including food, moisture, temperature, acidity, oxygen, and time.
snapshot.body:
Under favorable conditions, bacteria reproduce rapidly by dividing in half. The chapter states that under ideal growth conditions bacterial populations can double every 15–30 minutes, allowing one bacterium to potentially become approximately one million in fewer than six hours.

Important environmental conditions include:

Food — Protein-rich foods provide particularly favorable nutrients.

Moisture — Bacteria require available water.

Temperature — Warm temperatures encourage rapid growth.

Acidity or alkalinity — Many disease-producing bacteria prefer conditions near neutral pH.

Oxygen — Different bacteria may require oxygen, require its absence, or grow under either condition.

Time — Bacteria require time to adjust and multiply.

These conditions explain why controlling the food environment is central to preventing bacterial growth.

revisions.title: Foodborne Viruses Do Not Multiply in Food
revisions.content: Unlike bacteria, viruses require living cells to reproduce, so food usually serves as a vehicle carrying viruses rather than an environment where they multiply.

snapshot.title: Foodborne Viruses Do Not Multiply in Food
snapshot.mainIdea: Unlike bacteria, viruses require living cells to reproduce, so food usually serves as a vehicle carrying viruses rather than an environment where they multiply.
snapshot.body:
Viruses consist of genetic material surrounded by a protein layer and are smaller than bacteria. They cannot reproduce independently or multiply in food. They remain inactive until they enter a living cell, where they use that cell to reproduce.

Foodborne viral illness therefore generally results from contamination rather than viral multiplication in the food itself. Important contamination sources include infected people, food-contact surfaces, contaminated water, and contaminated seafood.

This distinction means viral food-safety controls depend heavily on preventing contamination through hygiene and sanitary handling

The chapter states that foodborne pathogens generally grow best from approximately pH 4.6 to 10, although individual organisms have different tolerances. Salmonella, for example, is identified as capable of growth between approximately pH 4.1 and 9.0.

In general, increasing acidity creates less favorable conditions for bacterial growth.
